SCHEMES, POLICIES AND PROGRAMMES 
 
4.1 Agriculture and Allied Sectors  
 
4.1.1 The Committee was informed by the Ministry that the Department of Agriculture and 
Farmers welfare ( DA&FW) is organized into 28 Divisions for coordination with State-level 
agencies and implementation of schemes in their respective fields. Further, one Public Sector 
Undertakings (National Seeds Corporation), nine autonomous bodies including Small Farmers’ 
Agri Business Consortium, National Horticulture Board, Natio nal Centre for Cold Chain 
Development etc., ten national level cooperative organizations and two authorities are 
functioning under the administrative control of the Department. Most of the central sector’s 
schemes related to Agriculture are implemented by DA&FW including Agriculture Infrastructure 
Fund, Mission Organic Value Chain Development for North Eastern Region (MOVCDNER) etc.       
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               
4.1.2 The major Schemes implemented by DA&FW to develop agriculture and farmers’ 
welfare in NER include:  
 
a) Pradhan Mantri Kisan Samman Nidhi  
The Pradhan Mantri Kisan Samman Nidhi (PM Kisan) is a central sector scheme under 
which financial support o f ₹ 6,000 per year in three equal instalments is transferred directly into 
the bank accounts of eligible farmers under Direct Benefit Transfer. The scheme became 
operational in December 2018. Under the scheme, State Government and UT administration 
identify the farmer families which are eligible for financial support as per the scheme guidelines.  
 
b) Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana 
The Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana (PMFBY) provides insurance coverage and 
financial support to the farmers in the event of fa ilure of any of the notified crops due to natural 
calamities, pests & diseases. The scheme also encourages farmers to adopt innovative and 
modern agricultural practices and stabilizes the income of farmers to ensure their continuance in 
farming activity. T he scheme is implemented by a multiagency framework by a few selected 
insurance companies under the supervision of the Ministry of Agriculture & Farmers Welfare 
(MoA&FW), Govt of India. 
 
c) Agriculture Infrastructure Fund 
The Agriculture Infrastructure Fund ( AIF) is a central sector scheme to facilitate the 
financing of agricultural infrastructure at the post -harvest stage i.e., farm gates and aggregation 
points.  The scheme was launched in 2020 and has a total outlay of ₹ 1 Lac crore. The scheme 
provides Interest subvention of 3% p.a., limited to ₹ 2 crores per project in one location, though 
the loan amount can be higher. The scheme also has a cap on lending rate, so that benefit of 
interest subsidy reaches the beneficiary and services to farmers remain affordable. 
 
d) Mission Organic Value Chain Development for North – Eastern Region 
The Mission Organic Value Chain Development for North Eas tern Region 
(MOVCDNER) is a sub mission under National Mission for Sustainable Agriculture (NMSA). It 
is a central sector scheme and aims at the development of certified organic production in a value 

31 
 
chain mode to link growers with consumers and to support the development of the entire value 
chain starting from inputs, seeds, and certification, to the creation of facilities for collection, 
aggregation, processing marketing and brand building initiative. 
 
e) Modified Interest Subvention Scheme 
The Government implements a modified interest subvention scheme to ensure that 
nominal interest rates are charged to farmers for short -term crop loans for agriculture and allied 
sectors. Under the scheme for FY 2021 -22, the lending rate to farmers and the rate of interest 
subvention has been kept at 7% and 2% respectively.  
 
f) Rashtriya Krishi Vikas Yojana - Remunerative Approaches for Agriculture and 
Allied Sector Rejuvenation 
The scheme was originally initiated as RKVY in 2007 to ensure the holistic development 
of agriculture and allied sectors by allowing States to choose their own agriculture and allied 
sector activities as per the State Agriculture Plan. It is a central sponsored scheme with a funding 
pattern ratio of 60:40 between the Centre and States and 90:10 for North Eastern States and 
Himalayan States. RKVY -RAFTAAR aims to make farming a remunerative economic activity 
through the strength ening of farmer’s efforts, promoting Agri -business entrepreneurship, focus 
on pre & post-harvest infrastructure.  
 
g) Mission for Integrated Development of Horticulture 
Mission for Integrated Development of Horticulture (MIDH) is a Centrally Sponsored 
Scheme for the holistic growth of the horticulture sector covering fruits, vegetables, root & tuber 
crops, mushrooms, spices, flowers, aromatic plants, coconut, cashew, cocoa, and bamboo. Under 
MIDH, the Government of India (GOI) contributes 60% of the total outl ay for developmental 
programmes in all the States except States in North East and the Himalayas, 40% share is 
contributed by State Governments.  
 
4.1.3 The Committee, in its meeting held on 27th February, 2023, discussed about various 
indigenous crop varieties in the NER. The Committee discussed about Boka Saul; an indigenous 
variety of rice produced exclusively in lower regions of Assam. It was discussed that this rice is 
not cooked conventional ly, as it can be soaked in warm or cold water, and after around 30 -40 
minutes, it is ready for consumption. It does not need any kind of fuel to cook. The Committee 
believes that the potential of this variety of rice can be tapped as it is not only nutriti ous but can 
be used as an alternate source of food in emergencies like flood, earthquake and disaster 
management. It could also be used for army and armed forces personnel posted in high altitude 
or remote areas.  
 
4.1.4 Further, the abundance of Bamboo in  NER and the viability of bamboo for commercial 
purpose was also discussed in the meeting of the Committee. Bamboo is not covered in the 
category of a tree after the amendment made to Indian Forest Act, 1927, and there is no 
prohibition on growing or cutti ng bamboo even outside the forest areas. This makes it easier to 
use Bamboo commercially. 
 
 
 
 

32 
 
Observation/ Recommendation 
 
4.1.5 Agriculture is one of the major sources of livelihood for the people of North Eastern 
Region and assisting and encouraging the farmers to continue their farming activities 
through the implementation of various schemes like Rashriya Krishi Vikas Yojana, 
Mission Organic Value Chain Development for North Eastern Region (MOVCDNER) etc. 
give impetus to agricultural development and upli ftment of the farmers in North Eastern 
Region.  The Committee appreciates the Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana (PMFBY) 
which is providing insurance coverage and financial support to the farmers in the event of 
failure of any notified crops due to natural c alamities, pest and diseases. The scheme also 
encourages farmers to adopt innovative and modern agricultural practices.  The 
Committee recommends that the Ministry of DoNER should make efforts that such 
schemes have a wider reach in NER and that maximum be nefits are reaped out of these 
schemes by the farmers.  
 
4.1.6 Taking note of the uniqueness of Boka Saul rice, the Committee believes that the 
potential of this variety of rice can be tapped. The Committee, therefore, recommends that 
special consideration may be given and efforts may be made to commercialize this special 
variety of rice and bolster its reach beyond the State of Assam. 
 
4.1.7 Similarly, considering the abundance of Bamboo in NER the Committee notes that 
its commercial viability has not been  fully tapped. The Committee, therefore, recommends 
that the Ministry may facilitate carrying out research activities in collaboration with 
various organizations well versed in this subject like the Indian Plywood Industries 
Research & Training Institute ( IPIRTI), situated in Bengaluru. This will enable the 
Ministry and respective States to utilize the immense potential of abundantly grown 
Bamboo in NER.  
 
4.1.8 The Committee further recommends that research on other indigenous crop 
varieties, such as beetl e nut, jackfruit etc. that are abundantly grown in NER, may be 
explored for its use for the welfare of not only the people of the region but also other parts 
of the country.

its own language, food, and cultural practices, which are beautifully represented through 
annual festivals such as the Hornbill Festival of Nagaland, the Sangai Festival of Manip ur,

4.9 Kaladan Multi Modal Transit Transport (KMMTT) 
 
4.9.1 The Committee inquired about the status of the Kaladan Multi Modal Transit Transport 
(KMMTT). The Ministry informed the Committee that KMMTT, a strategic connectivity project 
to connect the eastern ports of India with Myanmar has two components: (i) Waterways 
component and (ii) Roadways component. 
(I)       Waterways component: The construction of port and inland water transport was 
completed in December 2018. All works for the operationalization of the port have been 
  completed. Sittwe port is now ready for operationalization. A trial run from Sittwe port 
(Myanmar) was conducted successfully on 13 January, 2023.  
(II)      Road component: The Road component of KMMTT includes a new green field road 
project of 109.2 km to be built from Paletwa in Myanmar to Zorinpui on the India -Myanmar 
border (Mizoram) to double -lane NH specifications. The work was earlier awarded to the Joint 
Venture (JV) of Engineers Projects (India) Limited and C&C Construction Co.  Ltd. in 2017. 
However, due to slow progress and the bankruptcy of the lead partner of JV, the contract was 
terminated. Now IRCON International has been appointed as the New Project Executing agency 
for the execution of the project. The agreement with IRCO N has been signed on 7 th March 2022. 
IRCON has awarded the contract for 40 km stretch from Paletwa end (Myanmar) i.e. 0 km –40 
km and for 99 km –109 km (from Zorinpui end). Work has started in 0 km –10 km section (i.e 
from Paletwa, Myanmar end). Surveying and site cleaning works have started in km 10 - km 40 
section (Myanmar end) and 99 km –109 km (Zorinpui, Mizoram end). 
 
Observation/ Recommendation 
 
4.9.2 The Committee appreciates the efforts made towards the completion of the 
waterways component of the Kaladan Multi Modal Transit Transport (KMMTT), a 
strategic connectivity project to connect the eastern ports of India with Myanmar, and all 
the works that have been done for the operationalization of the port. The Committee notes 
and hopes that since a new  Project Executing Agency has been appointed for execution of 
the road component of KMMTT, similar commitment may be shown to realise the 
completion of road component of the project in a time bound manner.

the time-bound implementation of schemes considering the budgetary alloca tion available 
to them. The Committee further notes that the road sector schemes under Non -Lapsable 
Central Pool of Resources (NLCPR), Hill Area Development Programme (HADP) and 
North East Road Sector Development Scheme ( NERSDS) have been merged under one 
head of the North East Special Infrastructure Development Scheme (NESIDS) -Roads 
component. This will allow the Ministry to use the allocated amount of ₹ 2491.00 crores to 
prioritize their investments. Significant progress has been made in developing roadwa ys in 
the NER during the last couple of years. The Committee hopes that this merger of schemes 
will provide the necessary incentive for constructing roads in the unserved regions, hence 
stimulating economic growth in these areas.  
  (Para 2.2.4) 
Utilization of Funds 
The Committee notes that, in accordance with the Department of Economic Affairs' 
directives, a revamped mechanism for transferring funds under Central Sector Schemes 
has been implemented. The Committee  also notes that the Ministry has been able to utilize 
around 16% of the allocated amount in the first three quarters of the financial year. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry may strengthen its coordination 
mechanism with the NEC, States and implementing agencies so that such a situation, that 
arose in the Financial Year 2022-23, can be addressed promptly and without delay in order 
to maximize the utilization of funds.  The Committee also recommends that the Ministry 
make all-out efforts to ensure that the balance of ₹ 500 crores is accounted for by the close 
of the financial year 2022-23. 
 (Para 2.3.8) 
Capital Section 
  
 The Committee notes that due to a change in the c lassification of Head of Account 
under NESIDS, the major part of the budget outlay has been reflected under Capital 
Section. Hence, the total Revenue outlay has decreased to ₹ 1798.75 crores in BE 2023 -24 
from ₹ 2140.04 crores in BE 2022 -23.  The Committee  also notes that under the head 

47 
 
‘Schemes of NEC’, there is a shortfall of ₹ 381.58 crores in BE 2023 -24 compared to the 
projected demand of ₹ 1181.58 crores. The Ministry has also informed the Committee that 
allocated funds may not be adequate. The Committ ee, therefore, recommends that the 
Ministry coordinate with NEC to prioritize the expenditure out of the present budgetary 
allocation and seek more funds at the RE 2023 -24 stage to meet the shortfalls. The 
Committee also recommends that the requirement of additional funds under the Capital 
Section may also be realistically assessed at the RE stage and additional funds, if required, 
may be sought.  
 (Para 2.5.3) 
 
CENTRAL SECTOR SCHEMES 
 
Schemes of North East Council  
 
 The Committee notes the role of the NEC  in formulating regional plans for 
integrated and balanced socio -economic development of the NER. The Committee also 
takes note of the reply of NEC that the unspent balance of NEC schemes has been 
minimized and that much progress is being made. However, th e Committee is of the 
opinion that timely completion of projects is very important , not only because it prevents 
cost overruns, but also because its benefits pass on to the people of the North East. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that the NEC must be  proactive in facilitating the 
timely implementation of the projects. For this, NEC should minimize the queries and 
consider deputing their officers to resolve the issues involved through direct meetings with 
the State Government officials so that the impl ementation process is expedited. The 
Ministry, being the nodal agency for matters relating to the planning, execution and 
monitoring of development schemes and projects in the North Eastern Region, should 
closely coordinate with NEC to ensure the timely implementation of the projects. 
 (Para 3.1.7) 
 
With regard to the reduced allocation made for the Schemes of NEC, the Committee 
recommends that the Ministry may coordinate with NEC to prioritize the expenditure out 
of the present budgetary allocation and see k more funds at the RE 2023 -24 stage to meet 
the shortfalls. 
 (Para 3.1.8) 
 
Central Pool of Resources for North East and Sikkim  /North East Special Infrastructure 
Development Scheme (NESIDS) 
 
The Committee notes that in the fiscal year 2022 -23, the Ministr y has spent only ₹ 
0.17 crores against a budget of ₹ 650 crores under the North East Special Infrastructure 
Development Scheme (NESIDS). The reason given for low fund utilization is the 
introduction of a new process for implementing the revised procedure o f fund flow under 
Central Sector Schemes, as has already been discussed in the previous chapter.  The 
Ministry has stated that it expects to spend ₹ 1104.27 crores by the end of the Financial 
Year 2022 -23 for the schemes under North East Special Infrastruc ture Development 
Scheme (NESIDS), Non-Lapsable Central Pool of Resources (NLCPR) and Hill Area 

48 
 
Development Programme (HADP). The Committee observes that there is low utilization of 
funds in the first three quarters of the financial year 2022 -23. Non-utilization of funds may 
put additional pressure on the budget for the Financial Year 2023 -24. The Committee, 
therefore, recommends that the Ministry must take appropriate steps to ensure that its 
schemes are carried out on time in the forthcoming Financial Year. 
 (Para 3.2.9) 
North East Enterprise Development Scheme (NEEDS) erstwhile loan to North East 
Development Finance Corporation (NEDFi) 
 The Committee appreciates the performance under the North East Enterprise 
Development Scheme (NEEDS) and the loan provide d by the North Eastern Development 
Finance Corporation (NEDFi) for the promotion of micro, small, and medium enterprises 
(MSMEs) and microfinance sector which, no doubt, contributes towards more inclusive 
and equitable growth in the NER. The Committee woul d also like to commend the efforts 
to disburse about 92% of ₹  100.00 crores by 31 st December, 2022. The Committee notes 
that NEDFi has been designated as Central Nodal Agency for implementing the schemes. 
Hence, NEDFi now has a greater responsibility for m anaging funds for various schemes in 
NER. The Committee recommends that NEDFi, in coordination with Ministry of DoNER 
and NEC, must develop a robust and transparent mechanism for the transfer of funds and 
effectively streamline the ‘just -in-time’ disbursement of funds to maximise the benefits of 
the revised guidelines. 
 
 (Para 3.3.7) 
SPECIAL DEVELOPMENT PACKAGES 
  
Special Package for Dima Hasao Autonomous Territorial Council (DHATC) 
  
 The Committee understands that the efficient working of Bodoland Territo rial 
Council (BTC) , Karbi Anglong Autonomous Territorial Council (KAATC) and Dima 
Hasao Autonomous Territorial Council (DHATC)  would lead to socio -economic 
infrastructure development like roads and bridges, power, agriculture, art and culture in 
their resp ective territorial  regions. With the mentioned committed liabilities, the 
Committee finds that a significantly larger sum of ₹ 100 crores has been allocated under 
each of the heads for Financial Year 2023 -24. The Committee also notes that most projects 
sanctioned since ince ption under DHATC and KAATC are still pending completion. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry may take necessary action so that the 
identified infrastructure and development projects pending under these heads are 
completed in a time -bound manner. Further, the Committee would like to be apprised, in 
detail, about ongoing 10 projects under DHATC and the measures proposed to be taken to 
utilize the allocated amount under special package of BTC, KAATC and DHATC for 
development of these areas. 
                                (Para 3.6.3)  
 
 

49 
 
Prime Minister’s Development Initiative for North East Region (PM-DevINE) 
 
 The Committee takes note of the Ministry of DoNER's allocation of ₹ 2,200.00 
crores under the Prime Minister's Development Initiati ve for North East Region (PM -
DevINE) Scheme for the Financial Year 2023 -24. The Committee also notes that the PM-
DevINE would create infrastructure, support industries, social development projects, and 
livelihood activities for youth and women, creating in come and jobs. The Committee 
observes that this programme seeks to promote various development projects not limited to 
a single sector. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry may have a 
mechanism to closely coordinate with the NEC to monito r the pace and pattern of fund 
utilization of the various projects under this programme to prevent cost and time overruns. 
             (Para 3.7.8)  
 
 
PUBLIC SECTOR UNDERTAKINGS 
 
North East Regional Agricultural Marketing Corporation (NERAMAC) 
 
The Committee notes that, in BE 2023 -24, an allocation of ₹ 7.67  crores has been 
made for North Eastern Regional Agricultural Marketing Corporation (NERAMAC)  out 
of which ₹ 2 crores is for capital head and ₹ 5.67 crores is for revenue head. The Committee 
is of the considered view that various infrastructure faci lities related to agriculture and 
allied services need to be scaled up. This will promote Agri -Horti products, allowing them 
to reach their full potential. Focus needs to be given to augment support facilities like 
transport, storage, sale and profit gener ation even through the remote areas of the NER. 
The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Government consider improving 
infrastructure support for agriculture and related sectors.  
 (Para 3.8.7) 
 
North Eastern Handicrafts and Handlooms Development Corporation Limited (NEHHDC) 
 
The Committee notes that the North Eastern Handicrafts and Handlooms 
Development Corporation Limited (NEHHDC) has been successful in reducing losses over 
the years. The Committee believes that in this new internet age, promotion a nd advertising 
have found a new outlet through social media platforms. The penetration of various social 
media platforms to every nook and corner of the globe has solved the problem of last -mile 
reach. The Committee, therefore, recommends that social media  platforms may be used 
effectively to promote handmade products and showcase NER's unique art and crafts. This 
would also help the cause of the Make in India scheme, which has strongly advocated for 
manufacturing goods and services in India rather than sourcing them from other countries. 
The Committee also takes note of the resolution passed by NEHHDC to convert into a 
Section 8 company, 100% wholly owned by the Government of India, in accordance with 
the provisions of the Companies Act, 2013. As the matter  is under the consideration of the 
Ministry, the Committee recommends that the Ministry carefully consider this resolution 
weighing the benefits it will have on NEHHDC towards becoming self -sufficient. The 
Committee would like to be informed about the progress made on this account. 

50 
 
 (Para 3.9.6) 
 
SCHEMES, POLICIES AND PROGRAMMES 
  
Agriculture and Allied Sectors  
 
Agriculture is one of the major sources of livelihood for the people of North Eastern 
Region and assisting and encouraging the farmers to continue  their farming activities 
through the implementation of various schemes like Rashriya Krishi Vikas Yojana, 
Mission Organic Value Chain Development for North Eastern Region (MOVCDNER) etc. 
give impetus to agricultural development and upliftment of the farme rs in North Eastern 
Region.  The Committee appreciates the Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana (PMFBY) 
which is providing insurance coverage and financial support to the farmers in the event of 
failure of any notified crops due to natural calamities, pest and  diseases. The scheme also 
encourages farmers to adopt innovative and modern agricultural practices.  The 
Committee recommends that the Ministry of DoNER should make efforts that such 
schemes have a wider reach in NER and that maximum benefits are reaped o ut of these 
schemes by the farmers.  
 (Para 4.1.5) 
 
 Taking note of the uniqueness of Boka Saul rice, the Committee believes that the 
potential of this variety of rice can be tapped. The Committee, therefore, recommends that 
special consideration may be gi ven and efforts may be made to commercialize this special 
variety of rice and bolster its reach beyond the State of Assam. 
 (Para 4.1.6) 
 
 Similarly, considering the abundance of Bamboo in NER the Committee notes that 
its commercial viability has not been fully tapped. The Committee, therefore, recommends 
that the Ministry may facilitate carrying out research activities in collaboration with 
various organizations well versed in this subject like the Indian Plywood Industries 
Research & Training Institute (I PIRTI), situated in Bengaluru. This will enable the 
Ministry and respective States to utilize the immense potential of abundantly grown 
Bamboo in NER.  
 (Para 4.1.7) 
 
The Committee further recommends that research on other indigenous crop 
varieties, such a s beetle nut, jackfruit etc. that are abundantly grown in NER, may be 
explored for its use for the welfare of not only the people of the region but also other parts 
of the country. 
  (Para 4.1.8) 
 
 
 
 
Organic Farming in NER 

51 
 
 
The Committee notes that Sikkim has achieved the status of a fully organic farming 
state.  However, there is a need for dedicated machinery in NER looking into the capacity -
building mechanism of States and various agencies involved in agriculture and allied 
services towards strengthening  their organic farming infrastructure. The Committee 
recommends the Ministry of DoNER to provide its support and encouragement to other 
States of NER to achieve the status of an organic farming state. 
  (Para 4.2.5) 
Cold Storage facilities in NER 
 
The Comm ittee observes that,  out of 434  micro food processing enterprises in 
Assam with sanctioned loans under Prime Minister Formalization of Micro Food 
Processing Enterprises Scheme (PMFME), loans have been disbursed to only 252 micro 
food processing enterprises.  The Committee therefore recommends that the Ministry may 
take up the matter with concerned stakeholders  for timely disbursal of loans to the 
remaining micro food processing enterprises. 
 
 (Para 4.3.3) 
 The Committee notes the efforts taken by the Minist ry for the development of cold 
chain infrastructure. It feels that there is a scope for progress in the export and promotion 
of agricultural produce in different markets with the help of efficient cold chain storage 
and distribution facilities. The Committ ee further observes that two approved projects 
under Integrated Cold Chain and Value Addition Infrastructure Scheme of Pradhan 
Mantri Kisan SAMPADA Yojana (PMKSY) in the State of Nagaland are still under 
implementation as on 31 st January, 2023. The Committ ee therefore recommends that 
Ministry may coordinate with the concerned stakeholders  to take necessary measures 
towards operationalization of these projects at the earliest. The Committee further 
recommends that the Ministry of DoNER may take up the matter  with the Ministry of 
Food Processing Industries (MoFPI) for building more cold chain storage facilities with an 
efficient transport infrastructure support system which may boost the supply of products 
of agriculture and allied sectors into other markets. 
 (Para 4.3.4) 
Tourism  
 The Committee takes note of the Ministry of Tourism's efforts to promote tourism 
in the North East Region to make the region a preferred tourist destination. The 
Committee believes that there has been a post -COVID tourism boom aroun d the world. 
This can be best utilized by promoting tourism in NER. Every State in the North East has 
its own language, food, and cultural practices, which are beautifully represented through 
annual festivals such as the Hornbill Festival of Nagaland, the Sangai Festival of Manipur, 
the Behdienkhlam Festival of Meghalaya, and so on. Efforts may be made to make the 
journey and experience of tourists more comfortable and pleasurable so that more people 
want to visit these festivals and other attractions in th e North Eastern States. This implies 
that a seamless transportation infrastructure for tourists is required. There is also a need 
to develop a structure that allows tourists to experience this rich culture while also 

52 
 
preserving the autonomy of these tribal  areas. The Committee recommends that the 
Ministry of DoNER, in collaboration with the Ministry of Tourism, focus on developing a 
mechanism to foster healthy and holistic growth in the tourism sector, thereby boosting the 
NER economy. The Committee would a lso like to be apprised about the details of 80 
infrastructure projects worth ₹ 2598.15 crores relating to water supply, power and 
connectivity which may support the tourism sector in NER. 
 (Para 4.4.2) 
 
TRANSPORT AND CONNECTIVITY 
Roadways 
The Committee believes that completing road projects on time is critical to the 
economic development of NER. The Committee takes note of various road projects carried 
out in NER under various schemes. The Committee notes with satisfaction that all the 12 
road projects sanctioned under North Eastern States Road Inves tment Programme 
(NESRIP) have been completed. The Committee notes that physical progress on many road 
projects (>₹ 300 crores) expected to be completed between 2023 and 2024 is slow. Similarly, 
the Committee also notes that, few projects under the Schemes of NEC are yet to be 
completed. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry, in collaboration with 
the NEC and MoRTH, make efforts to identify and resolve bottlenecks that are delaying 
projects so that the benefits intended for the North East can be extended as soon as 
possible. 
 
 (Para 4.5.4) 
Railways 
The Committee takes note of the progress made towards completing various railway 
projects in the NER. The Committee recommends that the Ministry of DONER in 
coordination with the M/o Railways ensure that all ongoing projects are completed within 
the time frame specified to provide NER residents with railway c onnectivity. The 
Committee would also like to know the status of the currently sanctioned project to connect 
all State capitals in the North Eastern Region, as well as the status of all other projects 
undertaken by the Northeast Frontier Railway (NFR).  
 (Para 4.6.5) 
 The Committee also notes that the delay in completing the Agartala -Akhaura rail 
link project is due to issues with the contractual agency in Bangladesh and that the Indian 
side will be completed by June 2023. The Committee recommends that all efforts be made 
to complete the Indian side work by the projected date. Furthermore, the Committee 
recommends that the matter may be taken up with the Ministry of External Affairs for 
further discussion at a higher level, so that project work gets underway  on the Bangladesh 
side. 
 (Para 4.6.6) 
Waterways 

53 
 
The Committee notes the work carried out by the Ministry for the development of 
National Waterways in NER. It may be stated that North Eastern region has a large 
potential for regional connection through wat erways and this may be optimally reaped by 
the Ministry of DoNER and the Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways. 
 (Para 4.7.2) 
Civil Aviation  
The Committee notes the efforts of the Ministry of DoNER and the Ministry of Civil 
Aviation in constructing an d operationalizing a number of new airports in NER. North 
Eastern Region connectivity is a critical attribute for the region's overall development. The 
Committee also suggests that a similar impetus may be given and efforts made to 
operationalize the remai ning airports. This will help to promote tourism and last -mile 
connectivity in NER. The Committee would like to be updated on the status of the UDAN 
scheme's implementation in NER, as well as the frequency of flight operations and aircraft 
types used at these newly identified/operational airports. 
 (Para 4.8.6) 
Kaladan Multi Modal Transit Transport (KMMTT) 
 
The Committee appreciates the efforts made towards the completion of the 
waterways component of the Kaladan Multi Modal Transit Transport (KMMTT), a 
strategic connectivity project to connect the eastern ports of India with Myanmar, and all 
the works that have been done for the operationalization of the port. The Committee notes 
and hopes that since a new Project Executing Agency has been appointed for exe cution of 
the road component of KMMTT, similar commitment may be shown to realise the 
completion of road component of the project in a time bound manner.   
 
 (Para 4.9.2)

CHAPTER- I 
 
Recommendations/Observations which have been accepted by the Government 
 
1.1 Ranking of Police Stations 
Recommendation/Observation  
1.1.1 The Committee appreciates the initiative of ranking of police stations in the country. 
The Committee believes that the annual ranking of police stations work as a constant guide 
for improvements. It also provides a picture of the state of physical infrastructure, resources 
and deficiencies at the level of police stations. The Committee, therefore, recommends that 
the MHA may incentivize the best police stations in terms of funds and resources. It will 
recognize their hard work and create an environment of healthy competition among all police 
stations in the country.  
(Para 1.4.8 of 237th  Report) 
 
Action Taken 
1.1.2 The Annual Assessment of the Best Police Stations Scheme was undertaken since 
Year- 2017 to identify and recognize the ten best police stations of the country and also the 
best police station in a particular State or Union Territory.  
1.1.3 Report in this regard is released in the DsGP-IsGP Conference every year. There are 
two sets of awards given to police stations. The 3 best police stations selected for that year 
will be awarded ‘Shield’. Further, the top 10 police stations of the country and the top police 
stations of each State/UTs have been given certificates.  
1.1.4 Further, under the umbrella scheme of Modernisation of Police Forces, approved in 
September 2017, a component of “incentives for police reforms” was included in the 
implementation structure of the scheme of “Assistance to States for Modernisation of 
Police”.  It was decided to earmark a certain amount each year for awarding incentives to 
the State Government for the implementation of Police Reforms. To incentivize the 
implementation of police reforms as recommended by various committees, originally a 
provision of keeping up to 10% of the total annual allocation of the scheme was made.  This 
incentive fund has been increased to ‘up to 20%’ from the year 2019-20. 
Further Recommendation  
1.1.5 The Committee notes the reply.  
1.2 Training Mandate of Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
1.2.1  With regard to the training syllabi of the Academies, the Committee is of the firm 
opinion that the training syllabus should be dynamic and in sync with the changing need and 
times. A static syllabus will only make the entire training process redundant and a mere 
formality. The Committee notes that SVPNPA and NEPA do review the content of the 
training curriculum from time to time. However, the Committee recommends that a 
mechanism may be developed to review and update the training curriculum biennially/ 
triennially based on the professional requirement and ground-level assessment of the POs. 
(Para 2.2.19 ibid) 

 
3 
 
Action Taken  
 
 Action Taken Report from SVPNPA:- 
 
1.2.2 Regular review of syllabus and teaching methodology takes place. Academy also has 
high-level Academy Boards comprising senior civil/police officers, eminent educationists etc., 
as its members. The Board is headed by the Union Home Secretary. The Board periodically 
(once in three years) reviews inter-alia the syllabi and training methodology of various 
courses conducted in the Academy. 
 
1.2.3 On the basis of recommendations of the 37th Board meeting and the 39th Board 
meeting of SVPNPA Board, the Academy conducted a comprehensive Training Needs 
Analysis (TNA) in the year 2020. It is proposed to conduct the TNA exercise once every five 
years. 
 
1.2.4 For all the Mid-Career Training Programme (MCTP) Course guiding principle for 
the design of the course is the recommendations of Dr. Trinath Mishra, IPS (Retd.) 
Committee Report. 
 
1.2.5 However, as recommended by Hon’ble Committee that “a mechanism may be 
developed review and update the training curriculum biennially triennially based on the 
professional requirement and ground level assessment of the POs” will be ensured. 
 
1.2.6 These recommendations will be given due importance while designing the next MCTP 
Course. Contemporary topics like the Dark Net, Crypto Currencies, Drones, Big Data 
Analytics & use of Technology for better policing have been made an integral part of the 
Course Design. 
 
 Action Taken Report from NEPA :- 
 
1.2.7 NEPA is making constant efforts to keep abreast with the evolving challenges in the 
field of policing. All modern topics related to policing are incorporated in the syllabus, as 
and when required. In addition, eminent resource personnel from respective fields from all 
over the country, are invited to enlighten the trainees on the trending topics. 
 
1.2.8 In a bid to further improve training, North Eastern Police Academy (NEPA) is 
conducting a Training Needs Analysis, wherein its faculty officers are deputed to member 
states to get a first-hand impression of the training requirements and also obtain suggestions 
from supervisory officers vis-à-vis their specific needs. NEPA will ensure to keep up the 
recommendations of the committee. 
 
Further recommendation  
1.2.9 The Committee notes the commitment of the SVPNPA to develop a mechanism 
to review and update the training curriculum biennially/ triennially based on the 
professional requirement and ground-level assessment of the POs and designing the 
next Mid-Career Training Programme (MCTP) Course as per the recommendation of 
the Committee. The Committee further recommends that the training curriculum for 
the personnel should be developed in a hybrid mode – a mix of online and offline 
modules.

1.3 Training on Arrest and Interrogation Techniques 
Recommendation/Observation  
1.3.1 The Committee recommends that the MHA may advise States/UTs to impart adequate 
training to the police personnel on the procedure during arrests. The training should also 
emphasize that the rights of the detainee are not violated by resorting to manhandling during 
arrests. The police personnel should also be trained to understand  that their role is not just to 
arrest people but also to protect people and deter crime.  
(Para 2.7.4  ibid) 
Action Taken 
1.3.2 The Advanced Course on Investigation and Detection of Crime (10 Weeks) includes 
sessions on Arrest and related topics (A part of a module on Law, Police Procedure and 
Report Writing) (4 days). 
1.3.3 The subjects covered are: 
• Arrest – (D.K. Basu Vs. State of West Bengal) Remand prayer 
• Hand cuffing 
• Test Identification (TI) Parade 
• Bail 
• Legal Provision. 
1.3.4 Further, BPR&D is regularly conducting webinar, symposium, conference etc. with 
stakeholders which include officers from State Government. 
Further Recommendation  
1.3.5 The Committee notes the reply.    
Recommendation/Observation 
1.3.6 The Committee also recommends that the MHA may advise States to sensitize the 
investigating officers to use relevant provisions under the penal laws while registering a case 
and precautions be taken during trial to secure conviction. 
(Para 2.7.6  ibid) 
Action Taken 
1.3.7 “Police” is a State subject falling in List-II (State List) of the Seventh Schedule of the 
Constitution of India. It is primarily the responsibility of the State Governments/UT 
Administrations to maintain law and order, including investigation, registration and 
prosecution of crimes, protection of life and property, etc. Police Forces of the States work 
within the existing legal and institutional framework. 
 
 
 

 
5 
 
Further Recommendation  
1.3.8 The Committee notes that due to lack of knowledge of procedure among ground 
level police personnel, unknowingly, loopholes are generated in the process of 
investigation, collection of evidence, filing of charge-sheets which are taken advantage 
by the culprits.  This leads to State prosecution losing a lot of cases in the courts.  This is 
a undeniable fact in respect of all States/UTs.  Hence, the Committee desires that while 
centre may refrain from involving in day to day administrative matters of police   
enforcement of law and order, it ought to device a mechanism by making/amending the 
existing provisions suitably so that the training of police personnel from the level of 
constable to the level of SHO by States/UTs can be standardized so far as procedure on 
inter-state registration of cases and prosecution of crimes is concerned.  The Committee 
believes this could strengthen the law and orders system in the country to prevent 
criminals operating inter-state and taking advantage of loopholes to escape prosecution  
 
1.4 Creation of Dedicated Reserve Training Pool 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
1.4.1 The Committee observes that most of the time, police stations are understaffed, and 
when the officials are summoned for training, they don’t get relieved on time. As a result, if 
the training slot is for 100 constables, only 50 to 60 percent of the constables are allowed to 
take training. Therefore, the Committee recommends that MHA may advise States/UTs for 
creation of a reserved training pool at the District level so that if training is proposed to be 
given to 100 constables, then those chosen for training could be replaced with reserve 
constables from the training pool created for the purpose and there is no hesitancy on the part 
of the higher police officers in sending the personnel for training. 
(Para 2.11.3  ibid) 
 
Action Taken 
1.4.2 “Police” is a State subject falling in List-II (State List) of the Seventh Schedule of the 
Constitution of India.  It is primarily the responsibility of the State Governments to fill up the 
vacancies in the police force in their respective States.   The Centre also issues advisories 
from time to time to the States for filling up these vacancies in the States and to bring in the 
requisite reforms in the police administration to meet the lawful expectations of the people. In 
case the vacant posts of police personnel are filled by the States/UTs, the reserved training 
pool will automatically be created in a comprehensive manner.  
Further Recommendation  
1.4.3 The Committee notes the reply.  
1.5 Scheme for Modernisation of State Police Forces 
Recommendation/Observation 
1.5.1  The Committee appreciates the component of “incentives for police reforms” under 
the scheme of “Assistance to States for Modernisation of Police”.  The Committee notes that 
the incentive fund has been increased to up to 20% from the year 2019-20. The Committee 
however opines that the progress in police reforms has been slow and hopes that the 
incentives given to better performing States for taking various measures on police reforms 

 
6 
 
will encourage other States to fast-track the efforts towards modernisation of their police. The 
Committee recommends that the MHA may put the information in public domain about the 
States that are leading and lagging in the modernisation process.  This will create a sense of 
competition and put pressure on the States lagging behind to perform better. The Committee 
also observes that the issues behind the under-utilization of funds by the States also need to 
be identified. Therefore, the Committee also recommends that the MHA should consider 
constituting a Committee which can visit the underperforming States and 
assist/advise/persuade them to utilize the funds in a planned manner; otherwise the situation 
in these states may take a long time to show improvements. 
(Para  3.12.4  ibid) 
Action Taken 
1.5.2 The information about the States that are leading in utilizing funds and taking 
maximum benefit of the scheme of ‘Assistance to States for Modernisation of Police’ has been 
published in the Annual Report of the Ministry for the year 2020-21.   
1.5.3  In so far as recommendations regarding the visit of officers to identify and resolve 
issues behind the under-utilization of funds by the States is concerned; stipulation is being 
made in the guidelines of the scheme so that the same can be institutionalized. Besides that, 
the Ministry issues reminders to the States and implementation is reviewed regularly through 
Review Meetings. Further, the ‘High Power Committee’, which approves Action Plans under 
the scheme also discusses issues related to the under-utilization of funds with the 
representatives of the State Government and State Police. 
Further Recommendation  
1.5.4 The Committee notes the reply.   
1.6 Use of Technology by State Police 
Recommendation/Observation 
1.6.1 The Committee observes that technology like artificial intelligence, big data, etc. can 
effectively help in mapping the crime hotspots and getting a digital footprint of the criminals. 
This can be used to deploy force more effectively thereby reducing/preventing crime. 
Artificial intelligence can be used to draw correlations between the types of crime, time, 
location, match fingerprints, facial images, analyze CCTV footage and recognize vehicle 
number plates, etc. Big data can be used to integrate and store data from multiple sources. 
This will help in developing a scientific approach to policing. The Committee recommends 
that the MHA may encourage and incentivize States to leverage technologies like artificial 
intelligence, big data, etc. for policing. The Committee further recommends that BPR&D 
may be tasked to make a compendium of the latest technologies used by the various State 
police forces and share among them. This will help the States to fight crimes in a coordinated 
manner. 
(Para  3.17.4 ibid) 
Action Taken 
1.6.2 This Ministry shares the same view. This Ministry will continue to leverage 
technologies like artificial intelligence, big data analysis, etc., for policing by the State / UT 
Governments under the scheme of ‘Assistance to States and UTs for Modernisation of 
Police’. 

 
7 
 
1.6.3 BPR&D regularly publishes a Compendium of Equipment purchased by various 
police organisations.  As recommended by the Committee, BPR&D has been asked to make a 
compendium of the latest technologies used by the various State police forces and share 
among them. 
Further Recommendation  
1.6.4 The Committee notes the reply. 
1.7 Emergency Response Support System (ERSS) 
Recommendation/Observation 
1.7.1  The Committee notes that Emergency Response Support System (ERSS) is a Pan-
India single number (112) based emergency response system for citizens in emergencies.  
The Committee recommends that MHA may advise States to create a state-of-the-art facility, 
recruit adequate staff and sensitize them to handle calls. Regular feedback may also be taken 
from the complainants on the service of ERSS. This will help in improving the performance 
of police and building trust with people. Efforts should be made to reduce the response time 
to extend help to the person in distress. 
(Para 3.27.3 ibid) 
 
Action Taken 
 
1.7.2 The ‘112’ Emergency Response Support System (ERSS) has been made operational 
across the country in 35 States/UTs in coordination with the respective States/UTs. 
Advisories have been issued to the States/UTs regularly to make the system more enabled for 
providing assistance in the shortest response time possible. 
 
Further recommendation  
 
1.7.3 The Committee notes the reply. 
 
 
1.8 Model Police Act, 2006 
Recommendation/Observation 
1.8.1 The Committee is concerned to note that the Model Police Act was forwarded to all 
the States in 2006 and even after 15 years, so far only 17 States have either enacted the 
Model Police Act or amended their existing Act. This shows laxity on the part of the 
remaining States. The Committee is of the view that adoption/ implementation of the Act by 
all States will help in creating a uniform police structure across the country. Therefore, the 
Committee recommends that the MHA may take feedback from such States to understand 
their perspective in the matter so as to advise them accordingly, for the adoption/ 
implementation of the Model Police Act, 2006.  
(Para 4.3.3  ibid) 
Action Taken 
1.8.2 “Police” is a State subject falling in List-II (State List) of the Seventh Schedule of the 
Constitution of India. It is primarily the responsibility of the State Governments/Union 
Territories (UTs) to enact the Model Police Act, 2006 or to enact it with suitable 

 
8 
 
modifications. The advisory in this regard has been issued to all the States/UTs vide letter 
dated 02.05.2022. 
Further recommendation  
1.8.3 The Committee notes the reply.  
 
1.9 Dual System Vs Police Commissionerate System 
Recommendation/Observation 
1.9.1 The Committee notes that some States in the country have created multiple police 
Commisionerates in their States, while some States having sizeable populations do not have 
any police Commisionerate. The Committee is of the view that the police Commissionerate 
system leads to faster decision-making to solve urban-centric issues. With the growing 
number of cities with a million-plus population, the Commissionerate system would be a 
better option to manage for management of law and order problems and complex issues. 
The Committee recommends that the MHA may advise States to consider establishing 
police Commissionerate system in cities having more than 10 lakh population as 
recommended by Mooshahary Committee. 
(Para 4.4.4 ibid) 
 
Action Taken 
1.9.2 The advisory in this regard has been issued to all the States/UTs vide letter dated 
13.04.2022. 
Further Recommendation  
1.9.3 The Committee notes the reply.  
 
1.10 Village Policing 
Recommendation/Observation 
1.10.1 The Committee opines that the village policing system needs to be strengthened in the 
country. Therefore, the Committee recommends that the MHA may coordinate with 
States/UTs to make arrangements for providing training to the members of the village 
policing system about their role and responsibilities to help the police in the maintenance of 
law and order in the rural area. The Committee also recommends that the BPR&D may 
undertake a study by collecting State-wise data on the village policing system in the country 
in order to make a proper assessment of the prevalence and performance of the village 
policing in the country. The Committee recommends that the MHA may encourage the 
State/UTs and incentivize them for setting up village policing system as it would reduce the 
burden of the local police stations at semi-urban, Notified Area Councils (NACs) and towns 
in policing, vigilance and crime prevention. 
(Para  4.5.5 ibid) 
Action Taken 
1.10.2 Research & Correctional Administration Division of BPR&D is preparing ‘Terms of 
Reference’ for advertisement for inviting research proposals on the topic. 

 
9 
 
Further recommendation  
1.10.3 The Committee would like to be apprised of the progress made in this regard.

1.12 Revisiting the laws 
Recommendation/Observation 
1.12.1     The Committee gathers that the MHA has constituted a Committee to review the 
Indian Penal Code, 1860, Criminal Procedure Code, 1973 and Indian Evidence Act, 1872. 
The Committee recommends that the MHA may discuss the matter with all the stakeholders 
including the States, keeping in view of the best global practices in policing and 
constitutional rights and safeguards of the citizens. The Committee would like to be apprised 
about the recommendations made by the Committee pertaining to these laws. 
(Para 4.16.4  ibid) 
Action Taken 
1.12.2 The Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Home Affairs, in its 
146th Report dated 23.06.2010, had recommended that there is a need for a comprehensive 
review of the Criminal Justice System of the country.  Earlier the Parliamentary Standing 
Committee in its 111th and 128th Reports had also stressed the need to reform and 
rationalize the criminal law of the country by introducing comprehensive legislation in 
Parliament rather than bringing about piecemeal amendments in respective Acts.  The 
Government agrees with the recommendations of the Department-Related Parliamentary 
Standing Committee on Home Affairs regarding the need to reform and rationalize the

from Governors, Chief Ministers of States, Lieutenant Governors (LGs) and Administrators

laws.  The Government is committed to bringing out comprehensive legislation taking into

Stakeholders.

1.12.3 The Committee notes the reply.

2.1 Training Mandate of Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) 
Recommendation/Observation

police training in the Country.

2.1.12  Action Taken Report from Sardar Vallabh Bhai Patel National Police Academy 
(SVPNPA), Hyderabad:- 
 
a.   Training Needs Analysis: 
The Academy has been revising the training content and methodology periodically 
keeping in view of the changing field requirements. As part of this exercise, the Academy 
conducted a comprehensive Training Needs Analysis (TNA) in the year 2020 with the 
objective to understand the gap in domain knowledge, skills and attitudes imparted during 
training to the IPS recruits at the Academy vis-à-vis the requirements in the field. 
 

 
13 
 
In this massive exercise, the Academy collected about 12000 responses from eight 
states (Assam, Delhi, Gujarat, Kerala, Odisha, Punjab, Rajasthan, and Telangana) by using 
customized questionnaires, not only from uniformed officers and personnel of all ranks 
(approx. 700 from each state), but also from the allied departments and citizens across the 
cross-section of society (about 400 from each state), from the IPS officers of previous ten 
batches (61-70 RR batch) and the trainer SPs/SSPs of IPS Probationers of the last five 
batches (66-70 RR batch). All these have been analyzed to identify the gaps in basic training. 
In addition, the responses of the National Security Advisor, Union Home Secretary, Senior 
Security Advisor, Director Intelligence Bureau, Director CBI, Secretary R&AW, Director 
General BPR&D, DGs of CAPFs (CRPF, BSF, CISF, NSG) and DGs of various state police 
formations (Assam, Chhattisgarh, Haryana, Karnataka, Maharashtra, Odisha, Punjab and 
Telangana) were also incorporated. 
 
Committees consisting of senior police officers and academicians were constituted on 
Indoor training, Outdoor training and Teaching methodologies for discussing the insights 
obtained from the Training Need Analysis to identify actionable points and suggest changes 
to be brought about in the Basic Course training. Subsequently, presentations were made 
before the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA). MHA has permitted the Academy to implement 
the findings of the TNA exercise for the Basic Course training of 73 RR Batch (2020 batch of 
IPS). 
 
b. Academy’s supervision during the District Practical Training: 
A system of appointing a faculty member as counselor to each of the IPS probationers 
is in place at the Academy. The faculty counselor will be in touch with the IPS Probationer 
during the phase 1 training at the National Police Academy, District Practical Training 
(DPT) at the corresponding cadre state of the probationer and during the phase training at 
the National Police Academy. 
 
Further, it is to submit that, the faculty coordinators remain in close contact with the 
probationer throughout his/her training and also remain in touch with both the probationer 
and Training SP through video conferencing. As suggested by the Parliamentary committee 
counselors have been visiting the probationers in the field and also getting feedback so as to 
improve training. 
 
c. Mentor scheme:    In addition to the above the National Police Academy started the Mentor 
system from 2020 onwards. 
 
All the states have appointed mentors to guide the officer trainees during the period of 
their District Practical Training and beyond. 
 
The idea behind the mentorship is that in the initial phases of getting used to the life 
of a police officer, the officer trainees face a lot of professional & personal dilemmas which 
need to be addressed for imparting the right values & attitudes for a career of integrity, 
professionalism and contribution to the society. 
 
Every state would have some officers, who have proven themselves in the field and 
are known for their professionalism and integrity. If some of these officers, in the rank of SP/ 
SSP / DIG, are appointed as the mentors exclusively (apart from trainer SPs) for the officer 
trainees, then grooming them during the DPT, and even thereafter, would progress in the 
right direction and these Mentors might be able to shape them in their own mould. This 
scheme has been operationalised from 73 RR. 
 
 

 
14 
 
d.  Ethical Dilemmas: 
The Academy follows a sandwich model of training where in phase 1 training for 46 
weeks is imparted at the Academy, followed by 29 weeks of district practical training at the 
respective cadre state. After the district practical training, the trainee will report back to the 
Academy for 12 week phase 2 training. Phase 2 training is the final part of the basic course 
training. In the phase 2 training, there is a special module conducted on clearing the ethical 
dilemmas faced by the IPS Probationers during the field training. All aspects including 
integrity, honesty, rule of law, compassion, welfare etc. are discussed in this module.

people, and dupe them of their savings but also well-known persons and celebrities. The 
Committee is of the view that specialized training is required to deal with the increasing 
cyber crimes in the country. The Committee recommends that the SVPNPA, NEPA should

2.6.14 “Police” and “Public Order” are State subjects, as per the Seventh Schedule of the 
Constitution of India. The States/UTs are primarily responsible for the prevention, detection, 
investigation, and prosecution of crimes, institutional set-up, raising awareness among the 
public about cyber crimes and capacity building of their Law Enforcement Agencies (LEAs) 
including deployment of adequate manpower to deal with cyber crimes. The LEAs take legal 
action as per the provisions of the law against the offenders. The Ministry of Home Affairs 
supplements the efforts of the States/UTs, through advisories and financial support under 
various schemes, to tackle cyber crimes. 
 
2.6.15 The MHA has rolled out ‘Cyber Crime Volunteer Framework’ as a part of cyber

State/UT LEAs before taking appropriate action as per the existing provisions of law. There 
is no discretion provided in the hands of a cyber volunteer. 
 
2.6.16 The MHA has launched the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal which provides 
for reporting of all types of cyber crimes, with a focus on cyber crime against women and 
children. The complaints reported, through this portal, are automatically routed to the 
respective LEAs for taking further steps, as per law and the laid down procedure & protocol. 
The State/UT LEAs are sensitized from time to time to attend to the reported cyber crime 
incidents in a time-bound manner. In addition, a module, ‘Citizen Financial Cyber Fraud 
Online Reporting and Management System (CFCFRMS)’ has also been operationalized in 
2021, for quick reporting of financial cyber frauds and for stopping the flow of funds, 
siphoned off by fraudsters. A Toll-free Helpline Number ‘1930’ has been operationalized to 
assist citizens, in their own languages, in lodging online cyber crime incidents and for quick 
reporting of financial cyber frauds on the CFCFRMS module. The calls made on the Toll-free 
Helpline number ‘1930’ land on the Helpdesk/Cyber Cell dedicated in the respective 
States/UTs.

3.2 Investigation of Cyber Crimes 
Recommendation/Observation 
3.2.1  The Committee expresses its deep concerns over the rising rate of cyber crimes in the 
country. As per the information provided to the Committee, it is seen that some of the States 
like Punjab, Rajasthan, Goa, Assam do not have a single cyber crime cell, while in Andhra 
Pradesh, Karnataka and Uttar Pradesh, only one/two cyber crime cells have been set up. It 
observes that each day, cyber-criminals are using newer methods and new modus-operandi to 
commit cyber crimes. Therefore, it is important for the police to stay updated on new modus-
operandi and technology trends adopted by criminals. 
(Para 3.21.9  ibid) 
 
3.2.2  The Committee recommends that MHA may advise States to set up cyber cells in all 
the districts. The States should map the cyber crime hotspots which will help in quick 
detection of crimes and taking proactive measures to prevent cyber crimes. 
(Para 3.21.10 ibid) 
 
3.2.3 The Committee also recommends to upgrade the existing cyber cells by setting up dark 
web monitoring cells and social media monitoring cells to tackle different types of cyber 
crimes. 
(Para 3.21.11 ibid) 
 
Action Taken 
3.2.4 Cyber space is a borderless, complex and dynamic environment. The complexity of 
digitalization allows criminals to take advantage in committing cyber crimes like financial 
fraud, ransomware, malware attacks, identity theft, data theft, privacy breach, etc. The 
increase in the number of internet users, clubbed with rapid digital service adoption and low 
cyber literacy has led to an increase in cyber crimes incidents across the country.   Evolving 
technology like, the Internet of Things (IoT), Artificial Intelligence (AI), Drones, etc., may 
bring new challenges to cyber space. 
 
3.2.5 “Police” and “Public Order” are State subjects, as per the Seventh Schedule of the 
Constitution of India. States/UTs are primarily responsible for the prevention, detection, 
investigation, prosecution of crimes and capacity building of their Local enforcement 
Agencies (LEAs) including, setting up of district cyber cell, dark web monitoring cell, social 
media monitoring cell, training of LEA personnel etc., to deal with cyber crime. The Central 
Government supplements the initiatives of the State/UT Governments through advisories and 
financial assistance under various schemes for their capacity building. The MHA has issued 
an advisory to all the State/UT Governments for setting up State and District Cyber Crime 
Cells, in each State/UT for the handling of all types of cyber crimes. Accordingly, all 

 
37 
 
States/UTs, including Punjab, Rajasthan, Goa & Assam, have also set up a dedicated Cyber 
Crime Cell as Nodal Point to handle cyber crimes. 
3.2.6 The MHA has established ‘Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C)’ to 
provide a framework and eco-system for the LEAs to deal with cyber crimes in a 
comprehensive and coordinated manner. 
 
Further recommendation  
3.2.7 The Committee notes the reply of the Ministry that dedicated Cyber Cells have 
been set up in all the State/UT Governments including Punjab, Rajasthan, Goa and 
Assam which did not have a single cyber crime cell earlier.  The Committee further 
notes that the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C) has been set up by the 
Ministry to deal with cyber crimes in a comprehensive and coordinated manner.   
  
3.2.8 The Committee recommends that the Ministry may encourage State 
Governments to identify cyber hotspots in their State and maintain data profile on the 
cyber crimes being committed in those hotspot and the measures taken to contain those 
crimes. This data in this regard may be collected by the ‘Indian Cyber Crime 
Coordination Centre (I4C)’ and shared with other States for framing of policies by 
them to tackle such types of cyber crimes.

4.12 Separation of Investigation from law and order  
Recommendation/Observation 
4.12.1 The Committee notes that only a few States have separated the investigation from the 
law and order duties of their police. The Committee is of the view that separation of 
investigation from law and order is important to maintain the accountability of the police and 
increase their autonomy in investigating crimes. Therefore, the Committee recommends that 
the MHA may advise the remaining States to create separate investigations and law and order 
wings in the police. It will lead to specialization and professionalism in the police 
department, speed up the investigation and secure the conviction of offenders. 
(Para 4.6.9 ibid) 
4.12.2   To address the shortage of staff in creating separate wings for investigation and law 
& order, the Committee recommends that the personnel of the rank of ASIs & head 
constables can be utilized for investigation of minor offences of simple nature after adequate 
training. 
(Para 4.6.10 ibid) 
 
4.12.3   The Committee notes that one of the reasons of low conviction rate is the lapses in 
the investigation. Therefore, it is important that regular monitoring and supervision of the 
investigation of cases should be done by senior officers. The Committee recommends that the 
MHA may advise States for the field visit of the senior police officers of the rank of 
SP/IG/DIG for on-the-spot assessment of investigation of cases. The SP/DSP should submit

Recommendation/Observation 
4.13.1 The Committee is of the view that the key factor in the success of prosecution is 
proper coordination between the prosecutor and the investigator. Therefore, the prosecution 
set-up in the States needs to be strengthened. The Committee notes that many States/UTs 
have not established the Directorate of Prosecution. The Committee recommends that the 
MHA may advise these States for establishing the Directorate of Prosecution within a time 
frame. 
(Para 4.9.4 ibid) 
Action Taken 
4.13.2 “Police” is a State subject falling in List-II (State List) of the Seventh Schedule of the 
Constitution of India. It is primarily the responsibility of the State Governments/UT 
Administrations to make the police force efficient and capable and its functioning more 
effective and transparent. Police Forces of the States work within the existing legal and 
institutional framework in the matter. 
Further recommendation  
4.13.3 The Committee notes the reply that establishment of Directorate of Prosecution 
is the responsiblity of State Governments/UT Administration and State police forces 
work within the existing legal and institutional framework.  The Committee, however, 
believes that MHA may advise the States/UTs who are yet to establish Directorate of 
Prosecution, to set up the same in their States for better coordination between 
prosecutor and investigator. 
4.14 Promotional Avenues of Constables 
Recommendation/Observation 
4.14.1 The Committee notes that according to MHA, the State Governments are responsible 
to ensure the career progression of their police personnel. However, the promotional aspect is 
a very important aspect of police reform on which the Union Government is in contact with 
the State Government. The Committee further notes that the system of promotion of 
constables is different in the States and observes that most of the States do not follow 
incentive linked promotion schemes or any kind of extraordinary performance-linked 
promotion schemes. The Committee recommends that MHA may encourage States to

Recommendation/Observation 
4.15.1  The Committee notes that 31 States/UTs have constituted Police Complaints 
Authorities at the State and District levels for looking into complaints against police officers. 
The Committee is of the view that the Police Complaint Authority should be established 
outside the police force. Therefore, The Committee recommends that the MHA along with 
the Ministry of Law & Justice may take up with States to ensure that the Police Complaint 
Authority should comprise of retired High Court Judges, retired senior civil servant/ police 
officers, eminent jurists along with the representation of women. The Committee also 
recommends that BPR&D may conduct a study to assess the effectiveness of the Independent 
Police Complaint Authority in States to check whether the complaints against police 
personnel have gone up or reduced. The study may also include the types of complaints 
against police personnel and action taken thereon.

INTRODUCTION 
Prisons play a crucial role in any society, serving as institutions designed to hold 
individuals accountable for their actions that have violated the law. The conditions, 
infrastructure and reforms within the prison system are vital aspects that determine the 
efficacy of the criminal justice system and the potential for prisoner rehabilitation. 
Examining the state of prisons and their circumstances becomes more important in th e 
context of India, a nation with a diverse and complicated legal system as jails play an 
important role towards the reformation of convicts. 
2. In the federal structure of India, the distribution of legislative powers between the
Central Government and the State Governments is clearly defined under the Constitution.
The Seventh Schedule of the Constitution of India enumerates „Prison/Persons detained
therein‟ as a subject matter under the State List (Entry 4 of List II). This means that the
State Governments have the primary responsibility for enacting laws, establishing
institutions, and regulating the functioning of prisons and persons detained therein within
their respective jurisdictions. The Central Government, on the other hand, has limited
jurisdiction in matters related to prisons. Despite the fact that the State Governments are
responsible for managing and administering prisons under the Constitutional provisions,
the Government of India has been regularly advising and assisting State Governments o n
issues relating to prison administration in light of the significance of prisons to the criminal
justice system.
3. Some of the important statutory frameworks, legislations, rules and regulations
guiding prison management are „The Prisons Act, 1894‟; „The Prisoners Act, 1900‟; „The
Transfer of Prisoners Act, 1950‟; The Repatriation of Prisoners Act, 2003‟; „The Model
Prison Manual 2016‟ etc. The colonial period Acts were enacted with a view to have a
uniform system of prison management in the country. The Prisons Act, 1894 defines a
„prison‟ and empowers the State Governments to make rules consistent with this Act on a
wide range of issues viz. accommodation for prisoners, separation and segregation of
prisoners, control and duties of prison officers, maintenance of prisoners, diet and clothing
of prisoners, prison offences, offence by prison subordinates, power to make rules etc.
4. Over a period of time various Committees viz - The Jail Committee, 1939; All India
Jails Manual Committee, 1960; Justice A. N. Mulla Committee, 1980; R. K. Kapoor
Committee, 1986; Justice Krishna Iyer Committee, 1987, etc. were constituted to
modernise the Prison Administration and to bring in reforms that suits the needs of the
changing times. Dr. W. C. Reckless, a United Nations Expert on Correctional Work made
a study on prison administration in India during 1951-52. The recommendations of all the

2 
Committees have been considered and incorporated in the Model Prison Manual, 2003 & 
2016. Besides, Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) also carries out interventions and 
implements schemes for prison reforms in the country.  
5. In order to meet modern standards for managing prisons, recently, an effort was
taken by MHA and has decided that the entire obsolete Acts needs to be updated a nd
revised. As a result, the Central Government decided to study and update the obsolete
Prison Act dated from the colonial era in line with current demands and correctional
ideology. This task was assigned by the Union Government to the Bureau of Police
Research & Development (BPR&D). The Bureau has reviewed those obsolete Acts in
consultation with the stakeholders with a view to revise it according to the changed socio-
economic and political conditions and to emphasis on „Correctional Administration‟.
BPR&D has recently finalised the „Model Prisons and Correctional Services Act, 2023‟
and it has been shared with the States/UTs with a view that the new proposed Act may be
adopted by the States/UTs with necessary changes and thereby repealing the obsolete Acts.
6. The infrastructure of Indian prisons has undergone some developments over the
years, but numerous shortcomings persist. Many prisons suffer from overcrowding, leading
to a strain on resources, compromised living standards, increased tensions among inmates,
lack of adequate healthcare facilities, sanitation and nutrition, outdated and dilapidated
buildings, limited access to recreational activities, lack of adequate mental health facilities,
very high numbers of undertrials in prisons, inadequate prison staff and limited facilities
for education & vocational training. These deficiencies hinder the reformation and
reintegration of inmates into society, perpetuating a cycle of crime and recidivism.
Additionally, reports of abuse, violence, and human rights violations within these
institutions have raised serious questions about the treatment and welfare of prisoners.
7. To understand the factors and challenges faced in the domain of prison reforms, the
Committee chose the subject 'Prison - Conditions, Infrastructure and Reforms' for an in-
depth examination of the gamut of issues related to the Prison Administration and
Management in the States and report thereon. The Committee, during the course of
examination of the subject, held six (6) meetings. It interacted with the representatives of
the Ministry of Home Affairs   and the State Governments of Assam, Andhra Pradesh,
Bihar, Chhattisgarh, Gujarat, Madhya Pradesh, Odisha, Rajasthan, Tamil Nadu, Telangana,
Uttar Pradesh, and NCT Delhi. The Committee also heard the views of some of the domain

on the issues of condition, infrastructure and reforms in prison system through a
questionnaire. The State/UT Governments of Andhra Pradesh, Arunachal Pradesh, Assam,
Bihar, Chhattisgarh, Gujarat, Goa, Haryana, Himachal Pradesh, Kerala, Madhya Pradesh,
