2.6 Vacancies in Medical Staff of CAPFs 
 
Observation/Recommendation 
 
2.6.1 The Committee notes that there is a vacancy of 25.42% in the Paramedical staff of CAPFs 
against the authorized strength of 4,420. The Committee feels that since the forces play an important 
role in search and operations, lack of adequate medical/ Paramedical staff may have an impact on 
the well-being of its jawans. The Committee, therefore, recommends that urgent measures must be 
taken to fill all the vacancies of Para -medical staff of the CAPFs in a time -bound manner. The 
Committee further recommends that the CAPFs may explore the feasibility of recruitment on an ad -
hoc basis till regular appointments are made for Paramedical staff. The Committee would like to be 
informed about the role of the Paramedics and medical staff in the forces and the ratio in which their 
deployment is made vis-a-vis the number of person in the various Police forces under CAPFs. 
 
(Para 4.4.3 ibid) 
Action Taken 
 
2.6.2 The filling up of the vacant posts of Paramedical staff authorized in direct recruitment quota 
is under process. The vacancy to be filled up through promotion is already under process which is 
likely to be completed soon. As of now, there is no provision f or recruitment of Paramedical staff on 
ad-hoc basis in Forces. Medical Officers, including specialists, though are being filled on 
contractual basis. 
 
2.6.3 The role of Medical and Paramedical Staff are as follows: 
 

 
27 
 
 Medical & Para-medical Staff in CAPFs pr ovide primary medical cover to the troops and their 
families. The hospitals in which they serve range from the Mini MI rooms in Border 
Outposts/FDLs to 10/20 bedded Hospitals in Battalion and also the 50/100/200 beds in CH/RH. 
 CAPFs Medical Officers provid e primary Medical care at Unit level to the troops and their 
dependents. In composite Hospitals, Specialists Medical Officers provide secondary medical 
cover. Apart from providing medical care, all the Medical Officers including Specialist Medical 
Officers take part in various recruitment procedures conducted throughout the year in various 
types of Medical Boards (Annual Medical Examinations, Review Medical examination etc) 
which are constituted for this purpose. They also provide medical cover during Elect ion Duties, 
Internal Security Duties, Disaster Management or any other duty assigned, as and when 
required. CAPFs Medical Officers are also deployed in areas like High Altitude Areas, Border 
Out Posts in desert areas or in other areas having adverse climat ic condition, where usually the 
Civilian Doctors do not want to perform their duties. They are also entrusted in providing 
Medicare to the AB-PMJAY patients reporting to them. 
 Paramedical staff is an integral part for giving medical support either at far f lung Border Out 
Posts of in any adverse climate as well as at LWE areas also. These Paramedical staff, 
especially the trained Nursing Assistant and Medics, are the backbone or the First Line Medical 
Care providers to the troops where Medical Officers are not immediately available, and during 
patient evacuation. Similarly, Lab. Assistants, Radiographers, Pharmacists, Nurses 
(Male/Female) are the integral part of any Composite Hospital. Trained Nursing Assistants and 
Pharmacists are the important supporting s taff in Unit Hospitals in CAPFs organizations. A 
Medical Set-up without these Paramedical Staff remains incomplete and Medical Officers and 
Paramedical Staff work hand- in-hand to render optimal medical care to the serving personnel 
and their dependents. 
 The available strength of MO/Paramedical Staff of CAPFs is not adequate to provide Medicare 
to the troops and dependents. 
 The following recommendations are proposed in the aforesaid matter: 
 To augment the strength of Paramedical Staff in all existing Hospitals. 
 To explore the feasibilities for appointment of Paramedical staff on contractual /ad- hoc/ 
outsourcing basis to reduce the deficiencies and help in better Medicare to the troops.

2.16 Modernization of Prisons 
 
Observation/Recommendation 
 
2.16.1 The Committee notes that in some cases, the prison staff including medical personnel of the 
prison hospitals have been found involved in arranging mobile phones and other contraband items 
for the prison inmates. This is due to the fact that the prison staf f stay posted in one prison for long 
period of time. It leads to collusion between them and the prisoners. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that the MHA may advise all the States to follow rotational policy for transfers and 
postings of prison staff including medical staff and set a maximum tenure for which a staff can work 
in one prison. The MHA may consider creation of a cadre of prison staff for the Union Territories so 
that the personnel are transferred to different UTs and will not stay posted in one prison of any UT 
for long period of time. This along with the technological interventions for the security of jail cited 
in the Para above, will help in curbing the use of mobile phones and other contraband items by the 
criminals inside prisons. 
 (Para 4.22.5 ibid) 
Action Taken 
 
2.16.2 The Ministry of Home Affairs, vide letter No. V -17013/11/2022-PR dated 2.5.2022, had 
already advised the States that to discourage complacency and corrupt practices in Prisons, Prison 
staff may be rotated on a regular basi s. They have been advised that the prison staff should be 
transferred to other jails on periodic basis. On the point of creation of a separate cadre of prison 
staff for the Union Territories, it is informed that the Ministry of Home Affairs had assigned th e 
responsibility of examining the feasibility of transfer of prison staff between the Union Territories 
(UTs) to the Bureau of Police Research & Development (BPR&D), who, after receiving responses 
from all UTs, had informed that there are various administr ative and procedural limitations 
regarding transfer of prison staff between UTs, such as difference in Pay Scales, Service Conditions, 
Allowances, Language barriers, etc. Also, NCT of Delhi and Puducherry are UTs with legislature 
and are guided by their own rules and regulations and therefore transfer of Prison Staff between 
UTs was not found practical and viable. 
 
2.16.3 The other recommendations of the Committee are noted and continuous efforts will be made 
to streamline the procedure.

REPORT 
I, the Chairman of the Committee on Home Affairs, having been authorised by the 
Committee , present this Twenty-fifth Report of the Committee relating to the Criminal Law 
(Second Amendment ) Bill, 1995•. The Bill seeks to further amend the Indian Penal Code 
1860, the Code of Criminal Procedure , 1973 and the Indian Evidence Act , 1872. 
2. In pursuance of the Rules relating to the Department -related Parliamentary Standing 
Committee , the Chairman , Rajya Sabha , in consultation with the Speaker , Lok Sabha , 
referred•• the Criminal Law (Second Amendment) Bill, 1995, as introduced in the Lok 
Sabha on the 21st August , 1995 and pending therein , to th e Committee for examination and 
report. 
3. The Committe e invited the Secretary , Ministry o f Home Affairs, to make a 
presentation on the various provisions of the Bill. Accordingly, he made a presentation 
before the Committee on the 21st November , 1995. During his presentation , he explained 
the salient features of the Bill and the circumstances necessitating the present legislation . 
4. The Committee took up clause-by-clause consideration of the Bill in its meeting held 
on the 22nd November , 1995. 
5. The Committee considered and adopted the Report in its meeting held on the 
4th December, 1995. 
6. The principal changes s uggested by the Committee in the Bill and the reasons 
therefor are set out hereinafter:-
Clause 2 
Clause 2 o f the Bill seeks to amend Section 220 of the Indian Penal Code, relating to 
punishment for corrupt or malicious commitment for trial or confinement by persons having 
authority. As stated in the Statement o f Objects and Reasons to the Bill, India became a 
signatory to t he Inte rnational Covenant on C ivil and Political Rights in 1979. Para 5 of 
Article 9 of the said Covenant envisages an enforceable right of compensation for illegal 
deten tion, etc. At present, there is no provision for payment of compensation to a victim of 
unlawful arrest or unlawful detention. To fulfil this obligation, an amendment is proposed in 
the Indian Penal Code, 1860, to make a p rovision for payment of compensation to such 
victims. In the proposed amendment, a limit qas been fixed that the Court may award 
compensation not exceeding the amount o f fine w hich that Court is empowere d to impose. 
The Committee, while appreciat ing the object of the proposed amendment, is of the view 
that there should not be any limit on the amount of compensation to be awarded to the 
victims. Rather, it should be propor tionate to the period of unlawful detention or 
confinement undergone by the victims. The Committee is also of the view that there should 
be a provision for payment of interest in the event of delayed payment of compensation 
amount. The Committee recommends that Clause 2 be amended accordingly. ·

INTRODUCTION 
 
I, the Chairman of the Department -related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Home 
Affairs, having been authorized by the Committee to submit the Report on its behalf, do hereby 
present this Two Hundred Fiftieth Report on Action Taken by Government on the 
observations/recommendations contained in the Two Hundred Forty Third Report of the Committee 
on Demands for Grants (2023- 24) of the Ministry of Development of North Eastern Region 
(DoNER). 
 
2. The Two Hundred Forty Third Report of the Department -related Parliamentary Standing 
Committee on Home Affairs was presented to the Rajya Sabha on 17th March, 2023 and laid on the 
Table of the Lok Sabha on 20 th March, 2023. After presentation of the Report, the copies thereof 
were sent to the Ministry of DoNER on 20th March, 2023 requesting them to furnish Action Taken 
Notes on the recommendations of the Committee contained in the Report. The Ministry of DoNER 
furnished the Action Taken Notes (in English) on 4 th July, 2023 and (in Hindi) on 12 th July, 2023 
on the above mentioned Two Hundred Forty Third Report to the Committee. 
3. The statement on the status of implementation of the recommendations contained in the said 
Report of the Committee has been laid on the Table of Rajya Sabha on 27 th July, 2023 and Lok 
Sabha on 31st July, 2023 in pursuant to the direction of Chairman, Rajya Sabha dated 24th September, 
2004. 
 
4. The Committee considered the draft Two Hundred Fiftieth Report and adopted the same at 
its meeting held on 5th December, 2023. 
 
5. The recommendations/observations of the Committee are printed in bold letters.

Development of North Eastern Region on the recommendations contained in the Two Hundred 
Forty Third Report of the Committee on Demands for Grants (2023 -24) of the Ministry. The 
Two Hundred Forty Third Report was presented to Rajya Sabha on 17th March, 2023 and laid on 
the Table of Lok Sabha, on 20th March, 2023.

recommendations contained in the Two Hundred Forty Third Report have been categorized as 
follows:

Two Hundred Forty Third Report.

CHAPTER I 
Recommendations/Observations which have been accepted by the Government 
1.1 Utilization of Funds 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
1.1.1 The Committee notes that, in accordance with the Department of Economic Affairs' 
directives, a revamped mechanism for transferring funds under Central Sector Schemes has been 
implemented. The Committee also notes that the Ministry has been able to utilize around 16% of 
the allocated amount in the first three quarters of the financial year. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that the Ministry may strengthen its coordination mechanism with the NEC, States 
and implementing agencies so that such a situation that arose in the Financial Year 2022 -23 can 
be addressed promptly and without delay in order to maximize the utilization of f unds. The 
Committee also recommends that the Ministry make all-out efforts to ensure that the balance of ₹ 
500 crores is accounted for by the close of the financial year 2022-23. 
(Para 2.3.8 ibid) 
Action Taken 
 
1.1.2 The observations of the Committee are noted for compliance. 
 
1.1.3 Further, due to the CNA system being brought into effect, in this transition period 2022-  
23, there were two sources of funds for the Schemes of Ministry for the States – from the unspent 
balances of releases made previously; and from the budgetary outlays in RE 2022- 23. In 
addition to the ₹ 2,180 crore spent by the States out of the available balances from the previously 
released advances till FY 2021- 22; further expenditure/ utilization of about ₹ 1,295 crore was 
incurred from available unspent balances including from RE 2022- 23 by the SGs / IAs with 
pursuance from the Ministry of DoNER. 
 
1.1.4 Thus, the total expenditure / utilization in FY 2022-23 by the SGs / IAs in the NE Region 
amounted to nearly ₹ 3,475 crore. 
1.2 Capital Section 
Recommendation/Observation 
1.2.1 The Committee notes that due to a change in the classification of Head of Account under 
NESIDS, the major part of the budget outlay has been reflected under Capital Section. Hence, 
the total Revenue outlay has decreased to ₹ 1798.75 crores in BE 2023-24 from ₹ 2140.04 crores in 
BE 2022- 23. The Committee also notes that under the head ‘Schemes of NEC’, there is a 
shortfall of ₹ 381.58 crores in BE 2023- 24 compared to the projected demand of ₹ 1181.58 
crores. The Ministry has also informed the Committee that allocated funds may not be adequate. 
The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry coordinate with NEC to prioritize the 
expenditure out of the present budgetary allocation and seek more funds at the RE 2023- 24 stage 
to meet the shortfalls. The Committee also recommends that the requirement of additional funds 
under the Capital Section may also be realistically assessed at the RE stage and additional funds, 
if required, may be sought. 

3  
(Para 2.5.3 ibid) 
Action Taken 
 
1.2.2 The observations of the Committee are noted for compliance. 
 
1.2.3 Moreover, of the total expenditure of nearly ₹ 3,475 crore during 2022- 23, the capital 
expenditure accounted for 94% or about ₹ 3,260 crore – [inclusive of ₹ 600 crore from heads 
under Capital Section; and ₹ 2,660 crore for creation of capital assets from heads under Revenue 
Section]. 
 
1.2.4 For the year 2023- 24, it has been envisaged that out of the planned total expenditure of 
nearly ₹ 5,892 crore, the capital expenditure will account for 92% or ₹ 5,417.28 crore – [ 
inclusive of ₹ 4093.25 crore from heads under Capital Section; and over ₹ 1,324.03 crore for 
creation of capital assets from heads under Revenue Section]. 
 
1.2.5 However, the allocation for the overall holistic development, social infrastructure and 
social development targeted Schemes of NEC is ₹ 800 crore in 2023-24; (~20% higher than) ₹ 
666.87 crore, of the RE 2022-23. 
1.3 Schemes of North East Council 
Recommendation/Observation 
1.3.1 The Committee notes the role of the NEC in formulating regional plans for integrated and 
balanced socio-economic development of the NER. The Committee also takes note of the reply 
of NEC that the unspent balance of NEC  schemes has been minimized and that much progress is 
being made. For this, NEC should minimize the queries and consider deputing their officers to 
resolve the issues involved through direct meetings with the State Government officials so that 
the implemen tation process is expedited. The Ministry, being the nodal agency for matters 
relating to the planning, execution and monitoring of development schemes and projects in the 
North Eastern Region, should closely coordinate with NEC to ensure the timely implem entation 
of the projects. 
(Para 3.1.7 ibid) 
Action Taken 
 
1.3.2 The observations of the Committee are noted for compliance. 
 
 
1.4 Capital Section 
Recommendation/Observation 
1.4.1 With regard to the reduced allocation made for the Schemes of NEC, the Committee 
recommends that the Ministry may coordinate with NEC to prioritize the expenditure out of the 
present budgetary allocation and seek more funds at the RE 2023-24 stage to meet the shortfalls. 
(Para 3.1.8 ibid) 
Action Taken 

4  
1.4.2 The allocation under ‘Schemes of NEC’ at BE 2023- 24 is ₹ 800.00 crore against 
projected demand of ₹ 1181.58 crore. All efforts are being made to fully utilize the budgeted 
outlay. The shortfall of ₹ 381.58 Crore shall be taken up at RE 2023- 24 stage based on actual

1.5 Central Pool of Resources for North East and Sikkim /North East Special 
Infrastructure Development Scheme (NESIDS) 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
1.5.1 The Committee notes that in the fiscal year 2022 -23, the Ministry has spent only ₹0.17 
crores against a budget of ₹ 650 crores under the North East Special Infrastructure Development 
Scheme (NESIDS). The reason given for low fund utilization is the introduction of a new process 
for implementing the revised procedure of fund flow under Central Sector Schemes, as has 
already been discussed in the previous chapter. The Ministry has stated that it expects to spend 
₹1104.27 crores by the end of the Financial Year 2022- 23 for the schemes under North East 
Special Infrastructure Development Scheme (NESIDS), Non-Lapsable Central Pool of Resources 
(NLCPR) and Hill Area Development Programme (HADP). The Committee observes that there 
is low utilization of funds in the first three quarters of the financial year 2022- 23. Non-utilization 
of funds may put additional pressure on the budget for the Financial Year 2023- 24. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry must take appropriate steps to ensure that 
its schemes are carried out on time in the forthcoming Financial Year. 
(Para 3.2.9 ibid) 
Action Taken 
 
1.5.2 The observations of the Committee are noted for compliance. 
 
1.5.3 The need to ramp -up States’ implementing capacities t o measure up to the even higher 
budgetary resources mobilized for the MDoNER schemes for FY 2023 -24 onwards and any 
unspent balances upto end of FY 2022- 23 is being focused and impressed upon the IAs and the 
State Governments of the NE Region and being pursued along with right upto the highest levels. 
 
1.6 North Eastern Handicrafts and Handlooms Development Corporation Limited 
(NEHHDC) 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
1.6.1 The Committee notes that the North Eastern Handicrafts and Handlooms Development 
Corporation Limite d (NEHHDC) has been successful in reducing losses over the years. The 
Committee believes that in this new internet age, promotion and advertising have found a new 
outlet through social media platforms. The penetration of various social media platforms to every 
nook and corner of the globe has solved the problem of last -mile reach. The Committee, 
therefore, recommends that social media platforms may be used effectively to promote 
handmade products and showcase NER's unique art and crafts. This would also hel p the cause of 
the Make in India scheme, which has strongly advocated for manufacturing goods and services  
in India rather than sourcing them from other countries. The Committee also takes note of the 
resolution passed by NEHHDC to convert into a Section 8 company, 100% wholly owned by the

Government of India, in accordance with the provisions of the Companies Act, 2013. As the 
matter is under the consideration of the Ministry, the Committee recommends that the Ministry 
carefully consider this resolution weighing the benefits it will have on NEHHDC towards

this account. 
(Para 3.9.6 ibid) 
Action Taken

Recommendation/Observation

CHAPTER II 
Recommendations/Observations on which the Committee does not desire to pursue the

2.1 Scheme-wise projection viz a viz allocation of funds 
Recommendation/Observation 
2.1.1 The Committee is pleased to note that all the schemes of the Ministry have been  
approved up to the limit of 2025- 26 and feels that the additional time of 3 years available with 
the Ministry of DoNER may be enough to plan and execute its schemes. The Committee hopes 
that funds under the schemes can now be spent with proper planning and recommends that the 
Ministry prepare a road map in consultation with all s takeholders for the time -bound 
implementation of schemes considering the budgetary allocation available to them. The 
Committee further notes that the road sector schemes under Non- Lapsable Central Pool of 
Resources (NLCPR), Hill Area Development Programme (HADP) and North East Road Sector 
Development Scheme (NERSDS) have been merged under one head of the North East Special 
Infrastructure Development Scheme (NESIDS) -Roads component. This will allow the Ministry 
to use the allocated amount of ₹ 2491.00 crore to prioritize their investments. Significant progress 
has been made in developing roadways in the NER during the last couple of years. The 
Committee hopes that this merger of schemes will provide the necessary incentive for 
constructing roads in the unserved regions, hence stimulating economic growth in these areas. 
(Para 2.2.4 ibid) 
Action Taken 
 
2.1.2 The projects under the Schemes of Ministry of Development of North Eastern Region 
(MDoNER) are prioritized, selected and sanctioned as per the laid down procedure in Schemes 
guidelines in consultation with the stake -holders viz. the State Governments, Line Ministries to 
achieve the intended objectives. 
 
2.1.3 In so far as utilization of funds is concerned, MDoNER is fully complying with the revised 
fund flow procedure as per Department of Expenditure’s OM dated 9 th March, 2022 and various 
instructions issued thereafter. Funds are released on ‘just -in-time’ basis as per requirement of 
the projects. 
 
2.1.4 With regard to allocation of funds for NESIDS- Roads, the erstwhile NERSDS, an amount 
of ₹1100.00 crore budgetary allocation has been provided in FY 2023-24. Strategies are in place 
to fully utilize the annual outlay in a time bound manner. 
 
2.1.5 The objective of the NESIDS (Roads) will be to take up rehabilitation/construction/up 
gradation of roads (including bridges on the roads) in the NER falling under the following 
categories: - 
(a) Proposals inter se contributing to road connectivity to every block/sub -division HQ with 
the district HQ through already constructed Highways or roads. Preference to the 

8 
proposals which provide connectivity to the districts to saturate the related (Key 
Performance Indicator) KPIs of Sustainable Development  Goals (SDG) or 
Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI) either for the entire region or for multiple States 
or for an entire State. 
(b) Roads of strategic importance identified by Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) or Ministry
of Defense (MoD) or for major connectivity in areas of Autonomous District Councils.
(c) Replacement of timber/Bailey/temporary bridges having span more than 20 meters on
roads identified at (a) and (b) above.
(d) Proposals for providing Road/Rail and Water connectivity for economic centres or
tourist destinations, which is recognized by Ministry of Tourism/ITDC or falls on tourist
circuits developed by Ministry of Tourism/NEC.
(e) Proposals for providing connectivity to the remote villages which are out of ambit of
PMGSY.
2.2 North East Enterprise Development Scheme (NEEDS) erstwhile loan to North East 
Development Finance Corporation (NEDFi) 
R
ecommendation/Observation 
2.2.1 The Committee appreciates the performance under the North East Enterprise 
Development Scheme (NEEDS) and the loan provided by the North Eastern Development 
Finance Corporation (NEDFi) for the promotion of micro, small, and medium enterprises

2.4 Agriculture and Allied Sectors 
Recommendation/Observation 
2.4.1 Agriculture is one of the major sources of livelihood for the people of North Eastern 
Region and assisting and encouraging the farmers to continue their farming activities through the 
implementation of various schemes like Rashtriya Krishi Vikas Yojana, Mission Organic Value 
Chain Development for North Eastern Region (MOVCDNER) etc. give impetus to agricultural 
development and upliftment of the farmers in North Eastern Region. The Committee appreciates 
the Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana (PMFBY) which is providing insurance coverage and 
financial support to the farmers in the event of failure of any notified crops due to natural 
calamities, pest and diseases. The scheme also encourages farmers to adopt innovative and 
modern agricultural practices. The Committee recommends that the Ministry of DoNER should 
make efforts that such schemes have a wider reach in NER and that maximum benefits are 
reaped out of these schemes by the farmers. 
(Para 4.1.5 ibid) 
Action Taken 
2.4.2 Ministry of Agriculture & Farmers Welfare has informed that Government is promoting 
certified organic farming in value chain mode in all the North Eastern Region states since 
2015-16 through the schemes of Mission Organic Value Chain Development (MOVCDNER). 

10  
The scheme provides end -to-end support to farmers to develop their value chain from 
production to processing, certification and marketing. Under MOVCDNER, an assistance of ₹ 
46,575/ha for 3years is provided for the creation of FPO, support to farmers for organic inputs, 
quality seeds/ planting material and training, hand holding and certification. Financial 
assistance @ ₹ 32500/ ha for 3 years is provided to farmers for on- farm/off–farm organic inputs 
under the scheme. Under the scheme need based assistance is provided for various components 
namely Integrated Processing unit @ ₹ 600 lakh, Collection, aggregation and grading unit @ ₹ 
10.00 lakh, Integrated Pack house @ ₹ 37.50 lakh, refrigerated vehicle @ ₹ 
18.75 lakh, pre -cooling, cold stores, ripening chambers @₹18.75 lakh and transportation / 4 
wheeler @ ₹ 6.00 lakh. 
 
2.4.3 Since 2015-16, under MOVCDNER, 1.73 lakh ha area has been covered under organic 
farming by developing 379 FPO/FPCs involving 1.89 lakh farmers. In addition, 7 NE states have 
developed their own brands for organic products. So far, ₹ 886.16 crore has been released under 
the scheme. With the help of MOVCDNER and state -run schemes, Other North Eastern States 
are also expanding their areas under organic farming to transform into organic farming State. 
 
2.4.4 The flagship scheme of the Government namely, Pradhan MantriFasalBimaYojana 
(PMFBY) and Restructured Weather Based Crop Insurance Scheme (RWBCIS) were launched 
from Khari f 2016 season in the country. 27 States/Union Territories have implemented the 
scheme in one or more seasons since inception of the scheme. The scheme is optional for  
States. Therefore, States are free to opt in favour of the scheme. Five North- Eastern St ates 
namely, Assam,Manipur, Meghalya, Sikkim, Tripura have opted for implementation of the 
scheme. 
 
2.4.5 The following measures have been taken to increase the coverage and absorption of 
funds in NER States under PMFBY: 
• Financial sharing pattern between Centre and North Eastern States has been revised 
from 50: 50 to 90 :10 w.e.f. Kharif 2020 season. 
• Provision has been made for dedicated budget provision by insurance companies for 
Information, Education and Communication (IEC) including intensive publicity to cre ate 
awareness among the farmers. 
• To increase the dialogue and to impress NER States to adopt PMFBY/RWBCIS, 
dedicated nodals have been assigned under Technical Support Unit (TSU) of PMFBY. 
• NERAMAC also has been playing a very important role in various schem es for the 
benefit of NER farmers. It has also taken collaborative steps with various Government 
Departments like National Backward Classes, Finance and Development Corporation 
(NBCFDC), Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment, Ministry of Food Processi ng, 
etc through which NERAMAC strives to encourage farmers by promoting modern 
farming practices and also to develop value-added products. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
2.4.6 Taking note of the uniqueness of Boka Saul rice, the Committee believes that the 
potential of this variety of rice can be tapped. The Committee, therefore, recommends that 

11  
special consideration may be given and efforts may be made to commercialize this special 
variety of rice and bolster its reach beyond the State of Assam. 
(Para 4.1.6 ibid) 
Action Taken 
 
2.4.7 NERAMAC has been regularly supporting the farmers and entrepreneurs dealing with 
Boka Saul rice or Kumol Saul (as locally known) by providing market linkages. NERAMAC 
promotes this product through its retail outlets located as strategic places like airport, zoo 
premise, railway stations as well as at Dilli Haat, New Delhi. NERAMAC also promotes 
Boka/Kumol Saul/Magic Rice by displaying it at various events and export/buyer -seller 
meetsthat it participates in. The uniqueness of  Boka Saul is that it does not require cooking and 
can be consumed by directly soaking it in water for few hours. Going forward, NERAMAC will 
surely give special consideration and efforts to commercialize this special variety of rice and 
bolster its reach beyond the state of Assam. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
2.4.8 Similarly, considering the abundance of Bamboo in NER the Committee notes that its 
commercial viability has not been fully tapped. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the 
Ministry may facilitate carrying out research activities in collaboration with various 
organizations well versed in this subject like the Indian Plywood Industries Research & Training 
Institute (IPIRTI), situated in Bengaluru. This will enable the Ministry and respective States to 
utilize the immense potential of abundantly grown Bamboo in NER. 
(Para 4.1.7 ibid) 
Action Taken 
 
2.4.9 Bamboo is one of the sub- sector that has been covered under the “Agriculture Task 
Force” jointly formed by Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare and MDoNER to steer 
the growth of agriculture sector in the NER and efforts are being made in this direction. 
 
2.4.10 Through NEDFi, NEC has also finalized an “Action Plan for promotion of Bamboo in 
NER” in consultation with stakeholders and shared the same with Central Ministries including 
Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare and the NE States. 
 
NEC has also supported number of projects in this regard, some of them are:- 
1) Bamboo Development Project in Mizoram, Mizoram. 
2) Bamboo nursery raising and farming in parts of NER under AATMANIRBHAR BHARAT 
ABHIYAN (Arunachal Pradesh, Assam, Manipur and Meghalaya) 
3) Bamboo resource creation through plantation 
4) Promotion of commercial bamboo plantation in North East India etc. 
 
2.4.11 North East Bamboo Development Council (NECBDC) with its rich experience in the 
bamboo sector can play a vital role in facilitating research activities in identified areas that are 
stagnating the growth of the bamboo industrial activities. NECBDC is making arrangements 
with institutes like IITG, NID, IPIRTI (now, IWST) and other agencies to take up bamboo-related 
research and development relating to bamboo charcoal, bamboo shoot, bamboo handicraft and 
furniture, and constructions. It is also working with IIP (Indian Institute Of Packaging) on the 

12  
development of bamboo crates for the packaging of fruits and vegetables to replace plastic 
crates. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
2.4.12 The Committee further recommends that research on other indigenous crop varieties, 
such as betel -nut, jackfruit etc. that are abundantly grown in NER, may be explored for its use 
for the welfare of not only the people of the region but also other parts of the country. 
(Para 4.1.8 ibid) 
Action Taken 
 
2.4.13 NEC has supported projects for Arecanut cultivation through “Promotion of Arecanut 
plantation integrated with turmeric in the North Eastern Region of India (NERCRMS)” which 
has been sanctioned during FY 2022-23 
 
2.4.14 Village level arecanut processing units have also been established in Changlang District 
of Arunachal Pradesh especially for making of disposable plates under the initiation of 
NERCRMS (A society under NEC, M/o DoNER, GoI.) 
 
2.4.15 NERAMAC has recently taken steps to promote the indigenous crop varieties of NER and 
13 registered GI crops with the Company is one of the best examples of this. All these GI 
products are Agri-Horti items and fall under indigenous crop varieties. Moreover, NERAMAC is 
planning to roll out various projects to develop banana fiber, jackfruit chips, Assam lemon juice, 
etc. in FY 2023-24. 
 
2.5 Organic Farming in NER 
Recommendation/Observation 
2.5.1 The Committee notes that Sikkim has achieved the status of a fully organic farming state. 
However, there is a need for dedicated machinery in NER looking into the capacity -building 
mechanism of States and various agencies involved in agriculture and allied services towards 
strengthening their organic farming infrastructure. The Committee recommends the Ministry of 
DoNER to provide its support and encouragement to other States of NER to achieve the status of 
an organic farming state. 
(Para 4.2.5 ibid) 
Action Taken 
 
2.5.2 The “Action Plan on Organic Farming in Agri -Horti Crops” prepared by NEC through 
NEDFi is under consideration. In this regard, NEC has supported number of projects from time 
to time. 
Some of the recently sanctioned projects are: - 
• Turmeric Providing sustainable livelihood s cientific method of organic production of 
turmeric (Curcuma longa along with certification as organic produce C&RD Block, Ri - 
Bhoi district, Meghalaya. 
• Organic Tropical Fruit, Tamenglong 
• Organic Tea Cultivation in Tamenglong District, Manipur 

13  
• Promotion of Organic Plantation of Khasi Mandarin Orange in Meghalaya 
 
2.5.3 Also, NERAMAC has introduced two brands namely “Organic North East (One)” and 
NE Fresh” to promote the organic and natural products of NER. Moreover, as one of the 
implementing agencie s for the CSS formation & promotion of the 10,000 FPOs scheme, 
NERAMAC has formed and FPOs/ FPCs and encourages them to adopt organic/ natural 
farming techniques. 
 
2.5.4 Further Organic Farming is promoted in NER by Ministry of Agriculture & Farmers 
Welfare through the scheme of Mission Organic Value Chain Development (MOVCDNER). The 
details of the same may kindly be seen in reply to para 2.6.2 above. 
2.6 Cold Storage facilities in NER 
Recommendation/Observation 
2.6.1 The Committee observes that, out of 434 micro food processing enterprises in Assam 
with sanctioned loans under Prime Minister Formalization of Micro Food Processing Enterprises 
Scheme (PMFME), loans have been disbursed to only 252 micro food processing enterprises. 
The Committee therefore recommends that the Ministry may take up the matter with concerned 
stakeholders for timely disbursal of loans to the remaining micro food processing enterprises. 
(Para 4.3.3 ibid) 
Action Taken 
 
2.6.2 Ministry of Food Processing Industries (MoFPI) has informed that a total of 706 loans 
have been sanctioned to micro food processing enterprises in Assam (till 31.03.2023) under the 
Prime Minister Formalization of Micro Food Processing Enterprises Scheme (PMFME). Out of 
these, 389 loans have been disbursed. The micro enterprises are required to comply with terms 
& conditions of the lending banks and of scheme guidelines before disbursement of loans leading 
to gap between number of loans sanctioned and number of loans di sbursed. However, MoFPI 
pursues the issue of timely disbursal of loans to the remaining micro food processing enterprises 
with the concerned banks and also with State Level Banking Committee (SLBC) from time to 
time. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
2.6.3 The Committee notes the efforts taken by the Ministry for the development of cold chain 
infrastructure. It feels that there is a scope for progress in the export and promotion of 
agricultural produce in different markets with the help of efficient cold chain storage  and 
distribution facilities. The Committee further observes that two approved projects under 
Integrated Cold Chain and Value Addition Infrastructure Scheme of Pradhan Mantri Kisan 
SAMPADA Yojana (PMKSY) in the State of Nagaland are still under implementation as on 31 st 
January, 2023. The Committee therefore recommends that Ministry may coordinate with the 
concerned stakeholders to take necessary measures towards operationalization of these projects 
at the earliest. The Committee further recommends that the  Ministry of DoNER may take up the 
matter with the Ministry of Food Processing Industries (MoFPI) for building more cold chain 

14  
storage facilities with an efficient transport infrastructure support system which may boost the 
supply of products of agriculture and allied sectors into other markets. 
(Para 4.3.4 ibid) 
Action Taken 
 
2.6.4 MoFPI has informed that in order to create/augment the preservation and processing 
capacity including Cold Chain storage facilities in the country including Nagaland, MoFPI has 
been incentivizing setting up of cold chains units through Cold Chain and Value Addition 
Infrastructure scheme under Central Sector umbrella scheme Pradhan Mantri Kisan SAMPADA 
Yojana (PMKSY). MoFPI provides credit linked capital subsidy in the form of grants -in-aid for 
setting up such cold chain units to eligible entrepreneurs under the scheme. In order to attract 
proposals from North Eastern States under the scheme, a number of special incentives/ 
concessions is offered to such proposals vis -à-vis those located in general areas. A few such 
special incentives are as follows- 
 
i. Credit Linked capital subsidy in the form of Grants-in-aid is provided @ 50% of eligible 
project cost for difficult areas including NER (as against 35% for general areas); 
ii. The stipulated timeline for completion of project in difficult areas/ NER is 30 months against 
24 months for general areas. 
iii. Net worth of an applicant from NER needs to be equal to the grants sought (against 1.5 times 
net worth for general areas) 
 
2.6.5 MoFPI regularly follows up with concerned promoters for timely completion of the 
projects and handholds them in resolving issues/ clearances required by them. Details of Cold 
Chain projects assisted in Nagaland State under the scheme are as attached at Annexure –IV. 
 
2.6.6 Also, NERAMAC emphasizes on preserving Agri -Horti products with the help of cold 
storage units. NERAMAC is preparing for a collaborative approach with Bodoland Territorial 
Council (BTC) for setting up five solar/ hybrid powered cold storage in v arious districts of BTC. 
Moreover, NERAMAC is also exploring the option of setting up more such cold storages in select 
areas of NER 
2.7 Tourism 
Recommendation/Observation 
2.7.1 The Committee takes note of the Ministry of Tourism's efforts to promote tourism in the 
North East Region to make the region a preferred tourist destination. The Committee believes 
that there has been a post -COVID tourism boom around the world. This can be best utilized by 
promoting tourism in NER. Every State in the North East has its own la nguage, food, and 
cultural practices, which are beautifully represented through annual festivals such as the Hornbill 
Festival of Nagaland, the Sangai Festival of Manipur, the Behdienkhlam Festival of Meghalaya, 
and so on. Efforts may be made to make the journey and experience of tourists more comfortable 
and pleasurable so that more people want to visit these festivals and other attractions in the North 
Eastern States. This implies that a seamless transportation infrastructure for tourists is required. 
There is also a need to develop a structure that allows tourists to experience this rich culture 
while also preserving the autonomy of these tribal areas. The Committee recommends that the 

15  
Ministry of DoNER, in collaboration with the Ministry of Tourism, focus on developing a 
mechanism to foster healthy and holistic growth in the tourism sector, thereby boosting the NER 
economy. The Committee would also like to be apprised about the details of 80 infrastructure 
projects worth ₹ 2598.15 Crores relating to water supply, power and connectivity which may 
support the tourism sector in NER. 
(Para 4.4.2 ibid) 
Action Taken 
 
2.7.2 The observations/recommendations of the Committee are noted. 
 
2.7.3 In order to support tourism in the North Eastern Region, 80 projects worth ₹ 2598.15 
crore relating to connectivity, water supply and power supply have been sanctioned under the 
North East Special Infrastructure Development Scheme (NESIDS). Of these, 80 projects, 51 
projects amounting to ₹ 1647.01 crore relating to connectivity, 23 projects amounting to ₹ 
678.13 crore relating to water supply and 6 projects amounting to ₹ 273.01 crore relating to 
power supply have been sanctioned. Out of these, 02 projects amounting to ₹ 42.40 crore 
relating to connectivity, 03 projects amounting to ₹ 85.99 crore relating to water supply and 01 
project amounting to ₹ 20.96 crore relating to power supply have been completed. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
2.7.4 The Committee also notes that the dela y in completing the Agartala -Akhaura rail link 
project is due to issues with the contractual agency in Bangladesh and that the Indian side will be 
completed by June 2023. The Committee recommends that all efforts be made to complete the 
Indian side work by the projected date. Furthermore, the Committee recommends that the matter 
may be taken up with the Ministry of External Affairs for further discussion at a higher level, so 
that project work gets underway on the Bangladesh side. 
(Para 4.6.6 ibid) 
Action Taken 
 
2.7.5 Agartala-Akhaura Rail Link (Indian Side -5.46 km) is funded by MDoNER. Out of the two 
components on the Indian side, the Nischintpur Yard (under Phase -1) was completed in 2021 
and ready for train operations once the works on the Bangladesh side is completed. The physical 
progress of the Viaduct (under Phase -2), which connects Nischintpur Yard to Agartala main 
station, is 85% as on 30.04.2023 and efforts are being made to complete the work within the 
stipulated time. For the timely completion of the work on Bangladesh side (6.8 km being funded 
by Ministry of External Affairs), weekly review meetings are undertaken to monitor the progress. 
7th, 8th and 9th PSC meetings were held on 26 th July 2022, 15 January 2023 and 20 March 2023 
respectively. The next Project Steering Committee (PSC) meeting is also to be held shortly. 
Extension of Time has been granted till 30 th June 2023. The revised work plan has been 
submitted by Texmaco and verified by IRCON to complete the project by June 2023. 
 
2.8 Kaladan Multi Modal Transit Transport (KMMTT) 
Recommendation/Observation 

16  
2.8.1 The Committee appreciates the efforts made towards the completion of the waterways 
component of the Kaladan Multi Modal Transit Transport (KMMTT), a strategic connectivity 
project to co nnect the eastern ports of India with Myanmar, and all the works that have been 
done for the operationalization of the port. The Committee notes and hopes that since a new

3.1 Prime Minister’s Development Initiative for North East Region (PM-DevINE) 
Recommendation/Observation 
3.1.1 The Committee takes note of the Ministry of DoNER's allocation of ₹ 2,200.00 crores 
under the Prime Minister's Development Initiative for North East Region  (PM-DevINE) Scheme 
for the Financial Year 2023 -24. The Committee also notes that the PM -DevINE would create 
infrastructure, support industries, social development projects, and livelihood activities for youth 
and women, creating income and jobs. The Commi ttee observes that this programme seeks to 
promote various development projects not limited to a single sector. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that the Ministry may have a mechanism to closely coordinate with the NEC to 
monitor the pace and pattern of fund utilization of the various projects under this programme to 
prevent cost and time overruns. 
(Para 3.7.8 ibid) 
Action Taken 
 
3.1.2 In the PM-DevINE scheme guidelines, a robust monitoring & evaluation mechanism has 
been put in place to monitor the pace and pattern of fund utilization of various projects to 
prevent cost and time overruns. Specifically, Secretary, North Eastern Council (NEC) is a 
member of the PM -DevINE Empowered Inter -Ministerial Committee (EIMC) tasked with the 
following: 
• To recommend effect ive means for Monitoring and Evaluation through field inspection 
inter alia through suitable third-party agencies; 
• To review the progress of project implementation under PM-DevINE. 
 
3.1.3 In addition, the PM -DevINE scheme guidelines, also state that to limit construction risk 
(time and cost over runs), infrastructure projects should be awarded in Engineering-  
Procurement-Construction (EPC) mode, on fixed cost basis, with provision for liquidated 
damages. The tender notices and contracts may also include binding c lauses for incentives to 
contractors for early completion and penal provision for delay. In case of projects worth more 
than ₹100 crore, there should be adequate contractual provisions for concurrent monitoring of 
the projects by an independent third-party agency. All these provisions would limit cost and time 
overruns in PMDevINE projects. 
 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
 
3.1.4 The Committee notes the Ministry’s efforts in putting a mechanism in place to limit 
the construction risks of time and cost overruns  for the newly introduced PM -DevINE 
scheme. However, the Committee would also like to bring to the Ministry’s notice that, 
time and again, the implementation and completion of the infrastructural projects under 

18 
various developmental schemes have been affected by the slow pace of projects due to 
varied issues despite many such monitoring mechanism in place. The Committee would like 
to be apprised of the progress made so far for implementation of this scheme. 
3.2 North East Regional Agricultural Marketing Corporation (NERAMAC) 
Recommendation/Observation 
3.2.1 The Committee notes that, in BE 2023-24, an allocation of ₹ 7.67crores has been made for 
North Eastern Regional Agricultural Marketing Corporation (NERAMAC) out of which ₹2 crores 
is for capital head and ₹5.67 crores is for revenue head. The Committee is of the considered view 
that various infrastructure facilities related to agriculture and allied services need to be scaled up. 
This will promote Agri-Horti products, allowing them to reach their full potential. Focus needs to 
be given to augment support facilities like transport, storage, sale and profit generation even 
through the remote areas of the NER. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the 
Government consider improving infrastructure support for agriculture and related sectors. 
(Para 3.8.7 ibid) 
Action Taken 
3.2.2 NERAMAC has undertaken numerous activities to improve infrastructure support for 
agriculture and other related sectors. NERAMAC’s processing plants of cashew and pineapple 
in Tripura and Ginger in Meghalaya are in various stages of being made operational and are 
expected to be fully functional by mid-2023. Moreover, numerous primary/ secondary processing 
plants for value addition of NER Agri -Horti commodities are planned for FPOs in FY 2023- 24. 
Five Cold storage facilities are being set up in BTC, Assam at the request of the Council. 
NERAMAC is also initiating the process to enroll some FPCs to avail the Agricultural 
Infrastructure Fund supported and promoted by the Ministry of Agriculture  and Farmers 
Welfare. 
F
urther Recommendation/Observation 
3.2.3 The Committee notes the reply of the Ministry and appreciates the numerous 
activities taken to improve the infrastructure support for agriculture and allied sector. The 
Committee would like to be apprised of all the details pertaining to infrastructure activities 
being undertaken by NERAMAC in NER Region. 
3.3 Civil Aviation
Recommendation/Observation 
3.3.1 The Committee notes the efforts of the Ministry of DoNER and the Ministry of Civil 
Aviation in constructing and operationalizing a number of new airports in NER. North Eastern 
Region connectivity is a critical attribute for the region's overall development. The Committee 
also suggests that a similar impetus may be given and efforts made to operationalize th e 
remaining airports. This will help to promote tourism and last-mile connectivity in NER. The 

19  
Committee would like to be updated on the status of the UDAN scheme's implementation in 
NER, as well as the frequency of flight operations and aircraft types used at these newly 
identified/operational airports 
(Para 4.8.6 ibid) 
Action Taken 
 
3.3.2 The observations/recommendations of the Committee are noted. 
 
3.3.3 Updated status of UDAN Scheme as informed by Ministry of Civil Aviation (MOCA) is 
attached at Annexure-V

3.3.4 The Committee notes the reply of the Ministry. The Committee is of the view that

remaining length. TDC: March 2026.

sanctioned in February 2022.

Shillong, the capital of Meghalaya, with IR network:

crore and expenditure of `1070.77 crore has been incurred on the project upto 31.03.2023. An

execution is held up due to protest by the Khasi Students Union (KSU). TDC: Not fixed.

INTRODUCTION 
 
I, the Chairman of the Department -related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Home 
Affairs, having been authorized by the Committee to submit the Report on its behalf, do hereby 
present this Two Hundred Fifty First Report on Action Taken by Government on the 
Recommendations/Observations Contained in the Two Hundred Forty Fifth  Report of the 
Committee on  ‘Prison – Conditions, Infrastructure, And Reforms’. 
2.  The Two Hundred Forty Fifth  Report of the Department -related Parliamentary Standing 
Committee on Home Affairs was presented to the Rajya Sabha and laid on the Table of the Lok 
Sabha on the 21 st September, 2023. After presentation/laying of the Report, the copies thereof 
were sent to the Ministry of Home Affairs  requesting them to furnish Action Taken Notes on the 
recommendations of the Committee contained in the Report. The Ministry furnished the Action 
Taken Notes on the said Report to the Committee on 30th January, 2024 and additional 
information on 15th July, 2024.  
3. The Committee has noted that the statement on the status of implementation of the 
recommendations contained in the said Report of the Committee has not been laid on the Table 
of Rajya Sabha and Lok Sabha by the Ministry. 
 4. The Committee consid ered the draft Two Hundred Fifty First  Report and adopted the 
same at its meeting held on 6th  March, 2025. 
 
5. The recommendations/observations of the Committee are printed in bold letters.

follows:

above, in the succeeding Chapters. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

2 
 
 
CHAPTER- I 
 
Recommendations/Observations which have been accepted by the Government 
1.1 Women prisoners 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
1.1.1 The committee recommends that the babies born in the prison to be allowed to stay with 
mothers until the age of 12 in order to provide a nurturing environment for the children during 
their early years while ensuring their well -being and development. Further, as per guidelines 
issued from time -to-time emphasis should be given towards proper care of children relating to 
food, shelter, medical care, education, and physical growth. Apart from this, sports and 
entertainment facilities are also to be provided to these children.  
 (Para 2.4.7 of 245th Report) 
Action Taken  
1.1.2 ‘Prisons’/‘persons detained therein’ is a “State List” subject under Entry 4 of List II of 
the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution of India. Administration of prisons and prisoners is the 
responsibility of respective State Governments. 
1.1.3 The Report of the Committee has been shared with all States/UTs and they have been 
requested to take appropriate steps to comply with the recommendations made in the Report.  
1.1.4 The Ministry of Home Affairs has also issued an advisory to al l States and Union 
Territories forwarding the guidelines for the welfare of the children of women inmates. These 
guidelines, inter-alia, provide that the children of prison inmates should be provided access to 
education, recreational facilities, food, shel ter and medical assistance etc. The Model Prison 
Manual 2016 circulated by the Ministry of Home Affairs to all States and Union Territories also 
has a specific chapter on “Women Prisoners‟, which, inter -alia, provides that prison 
administration should ensure holistic development of the children of women inmates. The 
Ministry of Home Affairs had also circulated a report to the States/ Union Territories titled 
“Women in Prisons” prepared by the Ministry of Women and Child Development. The report, 
inter-alia, contains specific recommendations on “children of women prisoners” and “better 
living arrangements” for women inmates and their children, etc. 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
1.1.5 The Committee recommends that keeping in mind, the safety, hygiene, and health of 
women, adequate arrangements for separate toilets and bathrooms with proper water supply and 
more specialist women doctors are to be provided in women jails. The Committee al so notes that 
Ministry of Home Affairs should from time to time, instruct all the State Governments/UTs that 
necessary skill development programmes to be provided to the women prisoners which indeed 

3 
 
will help them to find employment after being released fr om the prison. It is also recommended 
that a study may be conducted on women inmates who have been released from jails to evaluate 
the effectiveness of rehabilitation programs, identify areas of concern and to enhance prison 
rehabilitation policy. 
 (Para 2.4.8  ibid) 
Action Taken  
1.1.6 The Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) has requested the Bureau of Police Research & 
Development (BPR&D) to undertake a study on women inmates who have been released from 
jails to evaluate the effectiveness of rehabilitation programs and provide its recommendation to 
MHA in a time bound manner.   
1.1.7 BPR&D has informed that there are five types of economic models for rehabilitation  
programmes designed for women inmates which are as follows: 
a. Economic Model 1: Vocational training programmes and educational  
programmes are conducted to empower the women inmates which will help  
them in starting their own activities 
b. Economic Model 2: Vocational training is provided to women inmates with the  
help of verified & reputed NGOs which in turn employ the women inmates after  
their release 
c. Economic Model 3: Discharged Prisoners Aid Societies (Non- govt. Company)  
have been established in some States which give financial loan to released  
prisoners for their employment 
d. Economic Model 4: Women inmates are given training and are off ered 
employment opportunities at the petrol pumps owned by the Prison 
Departments of the States 
e. Economic Model 5: Special Schemes are launched for rehabilitation and  
employment of released women prisoners 
 
1.1.8 BPR&D has further stated there are open prisons for women prisoners in 
some States which gives an employment opportunity to women inmates and prepare  
them for future employment once they are released from prison. It has been  
concluded in the report that the rehabilitation programmes for women inmates are still 
in transit phase and there is no uniform structure/policy in the regard. 
 
1.1.9 BPR&D has also informed that they, in association with Academy of Prisons  
and Correctional Administration (APCA), Vellore, are conducting a study on  
Stigmatization and Victimization of Released Women Prisoners and their Children in  
India and one of the objectives of the study is to “Study the measures, schemes  
available for rehabilitation, reintegration of women prisoners and their children in 
India”. It has been informed that the outcome of the above study will be shared once  
the research is completed. A copy of the study report of the BPR&D on the subject is attached at 
Annexure –A.  

4 
 
1.1.10 MHA has shared the recommendation with all States/UTs and has requested them to 
implement skill development programmes for women prisoners which will help in the 
reformation of inmates.  
Recommendation/Observation 
1.1.11  The Committee is of view that in spite of laws for the protection of women, it is often 
observed that women are subjected to discrimination in various stages of life, and if a woman is 
on the wrong side of law or being convicted for an offence, her miserie s increased manifold. As 
compared to male prisoners, female prisoners face endless problems. Since the prison 
administration and staff have wide discretion in their hands, the Committee, therefore, 
recommends that measures should be taken that their fundamental and basic human rights are not 
violated and they are being provided with basic necessities and respect available to a prisoner. 
Women only prison and women only staff should be the motto for all the State Governments to 
adopt. The Central Government may formulate necessary infrastructure development 
programmes in that direction.  
 (Para 2.4.9 ibid) 
Action Taken  
  
1.1.12 The recommendation of the Committee has been noted. 
1.1.13 The Report of the Committee has been shared with all States/UTs and they have been 
advised to take urgent necessary steps to comply with the recommendations made in the Report.  
1.1.14 The Ministry of Home Affairs has been issuing advisories to the States/UTs in this regard 
from time to time.  
1.2 Prison staff 
Recommendation/Observation 
1.2.1  The Committee has noted that across all categories of jail staff like -  jail cadre staff, 
warders, correctional staff and medical officers etc., the percentage of vacancies are very, high. It 
has become the most neglected part of the prison administration and it makes the management of 
the prisons very difficult. Having limited staff and making ad hoc arrangements to address staff 
shortage will compromise the security. A critical role is played by the Resident Medical Officers, 
Correctional Staff and Warders in the upkeep of the health conditions of the inmates, reformation 
and rehabilitation of the inmates and safety and security of the prison and prisoners. The 
Committee recommends that all posts need to be filled up immediately and no post should 
remain vacant for more than 3 months. 
 (Para  2.7.3  ibid) 
Action Taken 
1.2.2 ‘Prisons’/‘persons detained therein’ is a “State List” subject under Entry 4 of List II of 
the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution of India. Administration and management of prisons 
and prisoners is the primarily responsibility of respective State Governments. 

5 
 
1.2.3  The Report of the Committee has been shared with all States/UTs and they have been 
advised to take appropriate steps to comply with the recommendations made in the Report.  
1.2.4 The Ministry of Home Affairs has also issued advisories to States and UTs, advising them 
to make periodic assessment of the strength of all categories of prison staff and take immediate 
steps to fill up the vacant posts by conducting special recruitment drives. 
1.3 Women staff strength 
Recommendation/Observation 
1.3.1 The committee has noted that the States that house most of the prisoners are still below the 
benchmark standard set by BPR&D in the Model Prison Manual, 2016 in respect of staff to 
inmate ratio (1:6). Keeping this in view, the Committee recommends that all the State prison 
Departments should comply with the benchmark standards for the staff to inmate ratio as 
mentioned in the Model Prison manual, 2016. Non- compliance may lead to the compr omise of 
the safety and security of the prison and the prisoners.  
 (Para 2.8.4 ibid) 
Action Taken 
1.3.2 ‘Prisons’/‘persons detained therein’ is a “State List” subject under Entry 4 of List II of 
the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution of India. Administration of prisons and prisoners is the 
responsibility of respective State Governments. 
1.3.3 The Report of the Committee has been shared with all States/UTs and they have been 
requested to take necessary steps to comply with the recommendations made in the Report.  
1.3.4  The Ministry of Home Affairs has also issued advisories to States and UTs, advising them 
to make periodic assessment of the strength of all categories of prison staff and take immediate 
steps to fill up the vacant posts by conducting special recruitment drives. 
 
1.4 Training given to the prison staff 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
1.4.1 The Committee observes that training of prison personnel is very essential to enable them 
to have a dignified approach towards the inmates and to bring about reformation in criminals. In 
this regard, the Committee recommends that the training programmes co nducted by the State 
Prison Departments may be parameterized and their performance to be evaluated for providing 
funds. 
 (Para 2.10.3 ibid) 
Action Taken 

6 
 
1.4.2 The Ministry of Home Affairs has conveyed the recommendation to the Bureau of Police 
Research & Development (BPR&D) with the request to provide its report in the matter in a time 
bound manner.  
1.4.3 BPR&D has informed that to train the prison personnel, BPR&D has prepared prison 
training modules on the following parameters:  
•  Human Rights in Prison Administration 
•  Needs for Vulnerable Groups 
• Skill Development/Educational Programmes 
• Search Procedures 
• Stress Management 
• Leadership in Prison Administration 
• Managing Prison Industries

1.14.1   During its interactive sessions with various State/UT Governments, the 
Committee was informed that ganja and cell phones are the common contraband items

Government inform ed that throw method using catapult is one of the common 
approaches employed to smuggle the contrabands into the prisons. The Committee 
observes that the articles like cell phones inside the prison are used by the inmates to

prisons. MHA should set benchmar k frisking standards to curb the entry of contraband 
articles and in turn prevent gang wars. All the State/UT Governments shall comply with

to all States and UTs defines a “Young Offender” as any prisoner who has attained the age of 18 
years but has not attained the age of 21 years. The Manual has  a dedicated chapter on ‘Young 
Offenders” and provides guidance to States and UTs for treatment of ‘Young Offenders’. MHA 
regularly follows up the matter regarding adoption of the Model Prison Manual with all States 
and UTs so that the States and UTs can benefit from the guidance provided in the manual. 
Further Recommendation 
4.2.3 The Committee also advises the Ministry of Home Affairs to provide information 
regarding the studies conducted to understand juvenile offenders' social backgrounds and 
the recidivism rate. The Committee believes that conducting such studies  and taking 
appropriate measures based on the studies  shall help prevent youth from committing 
crimes.    
 
4.3 Prison Staff 
Recommendation/Observation 
4.3.1 The Committee observes that there are likely chances of jail staff colluding with the 
inmates in passing contraband articles into the prisons. Such corrupt practices in prison 
administration compromise the security and discipline in the prison. In order to curb such unholy 
nexus betw een the jail staff and inmates, the Committee recommends that strict 
penalties/disciplinary measures should be set in their conditions of service. 
 (Para  2.7.4  ibid) 
Action Taken 
4.3.2 ‘Prisons’/‘persons detained therein’ is a “State List” subject under Entry 4 of List II of 
the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution of India. Administration of prisons and prisoners is the 
responsibility of respective State Governments. 
4.3.3 The Report of the Committee has been shared with all States/UTs and they have been  
advised to take appropriate steps to comply with the recommendations made in the Report.  
Further Recommendation 
4.3.4  The Committee notes the reply given by the Ministry. Further, the Committee 
would also like to be apprised if the Ministry has issued a ny specific guidelines to the 
State/UT Governments to incorporate strict penalties/disciplinary measures in the service 
conditions of prison staff so that they would not collude with the inmates in passing 
contraband articles into the prison.    
 
4.4 Training given to the prison staff 

36 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
4.4.1 The Committee also recommends that a dedicated institute common to all the North 
Eastern States to impart correctional training to the prison personnel may be established. Each 
State should endeavor to establish its own training institutions exclusively for training jail staff.  
(Para 2.10.4  ibid) 
Action Taken 
4.4.2 The Report of the Committee has been shared with all States/UTs and they have been 
requested to take necessary steps to comply with the recommendations made in the Report.  
Further Recommendation 
4.4.3  The Committee notes the reply given by the Ministry. Further, the Committee has 
also noted that there is no dedicated training institute for imparting training to the prison 
personnel in the North Eastern Region. The States in this re gion are also excessively 
dependent on the Central Government for funds. Hence, the Committee further 
recommends that MHA may explore the possibilities for setting up one such institute in the 
North Eastern Region.    
 
4.5 Types of prisons 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
4.5.1 The Committee noted that many of the representatives of the State Governments who 
appeared before the Committee submitted that they are undertaking construction of new 
buildings, barracks and new prisons to accommodate the increasing number of prisoners. 
However, the Committee is of the view that these are not enough to address the overcrowding of 
prisons. In some of the States, the prisons are overcrowded to the extent of 185% of its capacity. 
The Committee, therefore, recommends there is a need for the State/UT Governments to 
undertake a comprehensive study covering the population of the region, nature of crimes, rate of 
conviction, crime rate etc., and accordingly come up with a suitable plan to enhance the capacity 
of the prisons and/or other alternative. Adequate fund may be allocated by the Central and State 
Governments for construction of new barracks, buildings and prisons as per the requirement.  
(Para 3.2.4  ibid) 
Action Taken

and prisoners is the responsibility of respective State/UT. 
4.5.3 The Report of the Committee has be en shared with all States/UTs and they have been 
advised to take necessary steps to comply with the recommendations made in the Report.

4.6 Prison Budget  
Recommendation/Observation 
 
4.6.1 The Committee has noted that very low sum of money is spent on prisoner welfare 
activities and 0.6% (₹ 13.16 Crores) on Vocational/Educational training of prisoners. The 
Committee recommends that the State Governments may create a Prison Development Fund. All 
the profits and other incomes accrued from the industrial activity undertaken by the Prison 
Department may go into such developmental fund. The amount in the fund may be used for the 
welfare activities of the prisoners which in turn minimize the dependency on the Budget 
allotment from the Governments.

and vocational training to prison inmates.

the issue with NIC for faster integration of CCTNS and e -Courts with e - Prisons which 
is going to benefit all the stakeholders like police, prison administration, prosecutors,

can obtain the benefits of ICJS.

Recommendation/Observation  
4.8.1 The Committee was informed by various State/UT Governments that the

presentations, it has been found that the wages/earnings which they are getting are very 
less. Hence, the Committee is of the view that it is essential to ensure that the wages 
paid to prisoners  are fair and equitable and that prisoners are not exploited for their 
labor. Therefore, the Committee recommends that the wages of the prisoners needs to 
be increased as this will help to improve the socio -economic conditions of prisoners and 
reduce recid ivism rates.

Types of economic models of rehabilitation programmes 
Designed for Women Inmates 
Economic model-I

T
o train the Prison Personnel and enabling them to have a dignified approach 
towards the inmates and to bring about the reforms in inmates, the following 
parameters have been laid down for the training programmes: - 
• Human Rights in Prison Administration : Prison Officers shall ensure that
while administering prison, human rights of prisoners are protected. On the
other hand, human rights of prison administration officers and staff are also
of immense importance. Prison personnel should understand the ways and
means of ensuring human rights protection through prison administration.
The rights of Prisoners shall be ensured according to international covenants.
International Legal instruments as well as judicial precedents of India
through which various rights of prisoners are conferred and ensured.
• N
eeds of Vulnerable Groups : The prison officers shall ensure the needs of
vulnerable groups. Prison officers shall be trained in identification of
vulnerable groups of prisoners and their specific issues and work towards
reducing the existing vulnerabilities by adopting and implementing positive
policy level measures.

48 
• Skill Development/Educational Programmes: Skill development of prison
inm
ates is a crucial activity that weans inmates away from  recidivism.
Theses programme is to explore and understand practical ways in which skill
development and educational courses could be undertaken in prisons.
• Rehabilitation and Correctional Programmes : Prison officers shall be
aware of knowledge and skills related to implementation of rehabilitati on
a
nd correctional programmes for the prisoners.
• S
tress Management: Prison Officers shall have necessary knowledge about
stress, sources, effects, management techniques, etc.,
• S
earch Procedures : Invasive body searches lie at the crosshairs of the
fundamental principle inherent under the human rights framework that the
treatment of prisoners should be humane and respect the inherent rights and
dignity of the person.
• L
eadership in Prison Administration : A variety of leadership
competencies are required in order to develop effective leadership in prisons.
A Prison Leader must be able to lead a team and motivate staff to work for
organizational goals and bring reforms and improvements in the prison
system.
• M
anaging Prison Industries: There have been several developments in the
establishment of new industries and the modernization of existing sectors in
response to market trends. Hence Prison Officers need to be trained on this
subject of managing prison industries develop modern Prison Industries or
m
odernize the existing ones.

ender Sensitization : Gender sensitive prison management policies and
practices should be responsive to the needs of women in a holistic manner.
Gender biases have to be challenged in all decision-making processes. Equal
and equitable treatment and participation of women in the correctional
system helps to promote diversity and inclusiveness and a safe environment.

mergencies in Prison Administration : Emergency preparedness is

anagement attention.

ynamic and Static Security in Prisons : prison officers must hav e

owledge and skill training related to physical, procedural and dynamic

Steps taken by Bihar Prisons to address HIV within prisons are as follows: 
Comprehensive health screening of the incoming inmates (within 48 hours of admission) facilitates the 
early detection of HIV -positive individuals. Subsequent to identification, a process of comprehensive and 
accurate diagnosis ensues, ensuring that appropriate treatment modalities are promptly administered to 
incarcerated individuals requiring medical intervention. 
2. Education and Prevention Programs: Inmates are educated on the importance of adopting preventive
measures and seeking timely medical intervention. Through these educational endeavours, incarcerated
populations are equipped with the requisite knowledge and skills to mitigate the risk of HIV acquisition and
transmission.

H
IV prevalence rates within correctional institutions are conducted to discern emerging patterns and enact
tailored interventions. This monitoring process encompasses assessments conducted both at the prison level
and centrally at headquarters, ensuring a comprehensive oversight of HIV dynamics within correctional
systems.

Plan India under BSACS (Bihar State AIDS Control Society), Bihar, Patna constitutes a concerted effort by
correctional authorities to forge partnerships with external healthcare entities. This facilitates enhanced
access to specialized medical care and comprehensive su pport services tailored to meet the unique needs of
HIV-positive inmates within correctional settings.

CHAPTER-I 
 
OVERVIEW 
 
1.1.1. The Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) is responsible for internal security, border 
management, Centre-State relations, administration of Union Territories, management of Central 
Armed Police Forces (CAPFs), Disaster Management, etc. While discharging its duties, the Ministry 
of Home Affairs continuously monitors the internal security situation, issues appropriate advisories, 
shares intelligence inputs, extends manpower and financial support, guidance and expertise to the 
State Governments for maintenance of security, peace and harmony without encroaching upon the 
constitutional rights of the States.   Though 'Public Order' and 'Police' are the responsibilities of 
States as per the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution of India, Article 355 of the Constitution 
enjoins the Union to protect every State against external aggression and internal disturbance and to 
ensure that the Government of every State is carried on in accordance with the provisions of the 
Constitution.  
 
1.2 Goals  and  Objectives 
 
1.2.1 The Outcome Budget (2025-26) of the Ministry of Home Affairs throws light on its goals and 
objectives. The MHA administers and implements a wide arch of schemes and programmes as 
mentioned therein in detail.  In brief, the goals and objectives of the Ministry for the year (2025-26) 
are as follows:- 
 
(i) Continuous monitoring of  internal security situation and issuing timely 
advisories; 
(ii) Implementing a zero-tolerance policy against terrorism and drug trafficking; 
(iii) Strengthening border management strategies to enhance national security; 
(iv) Promoting the modernization of the criminal justice system through new laws and 
digitization; 
(v) Enhancing forensic science capabilities to improve the quality of investigations; 
(vi) Developing an Inter-operable Criminal Justice System (ICJS) to facilitate 
seamless  communication between law enforcement agencies; 
(vii) Supporting disaster management initiatives to enhance preparedness and response 
capabilities; 
(viii) Fostering community engagement programs to promote peace, harmony and 
social cohesion; 
(ix) Implementing initiatives for women's safety and empowerment to ensure a secure 
environment for women; 
(x) Timely disbursement of funds for freedom fighters and their families; 
(xi) Ensuring the provision of security, administrative and residential infrastructure of 
CAPFs; 
(xii) Ensuring security and administrative infrastructure for Central Forensic Science 
Laboratories (CFSLs); 
(xiii) Enhancing training, capacity-building and skill development programs for police 
personnel to improve their skills and efficiency; 
(xiv) Supporting the holistic development of islands in Union Territories to enhance 
local governance and infrastructure; 

2 
 
 
(xv) Conducting regular census and surveys to maintain accurate demographic data 
and support policy formulation; 
(xvi) Reimbursement of expenditure under Security Related Expenditure (SRE) to 
States; 
(xvii) Special Infrastructure Support for Left Wing Extremism (LWE) affected States; 
(xviii) Fostering international cooperation on security issues, including counter-terrorism 
and transnational crime; 
(xix) Establishment of a Bhartiya Bhasha Anubhag to support translation services and 
promote linguistic diversity; 
(xx) Scheme for support to poor prisoners; 
(xxi) Modernization of prisons; and 
(xxii) Streamlining immigration processes through the Immigration, Visa, 
Foreigners Registration and Tracking (IVFRT) system.

2.1 OVERVIEW 
 
2.1.1 There are eleven Demands for Grants which are administered by the Ministry of Home 
Affairs (MHA). The detailed Demands for Grants of the Ministry of Home Affairs are divided into 
three volumes: Vol. I, Vol. II-A and Vol. II-B. The Detailed Demands for Grants (Volume-I) 
contains three Grants (Nos. 49-51), namely the Ministry of Home Affairs (Grant No. 49); the 
Cabinet (Grant No. 50); and the Police (Grant No. 51). 
 
2.1.2. The Detailed Demands for Grants (Volumes-II-A and II-B) relate to the five Union Territories 
(without Legislature), namely Andaman & Nicobar Islands (Grant No. 52), Chandigarh (Grant

No. 57- Transfers to Delhi), Jammu & Kashmir (Grant No.58- Transfers to Jammu & Kashmir) and 
Puducherry (Grant No. 59- Transfers to Puducherry). 
 
2.1.3 The provisions for the Union Territories (without Legislature) form part of the Demands of 
the Ministry of Home Affairs. However, various programmes/schemes are the subject matter of

Legislature) cover Assistance to the Union Territories of Puducherry, Jammu & Kashmir and NCT 
of Delhi, in the form of the Grants and Loans. In respect of these three Grants, the Ministry of Home 
Affairs releases the Grants on quarterly basis and has a limited role in scrutinizing, sanctioning and 
implementation of the schemes/projects.

police-related expenditures are lower than the projected amounts for BE 2025-26. Notable reductions 
are observed in the budgets for the Central Armed Police Forces (CAPFs), Central Police
